Preface
This book is the course material for the R course of the Quantitative Genetics and Statistical Learning Lab (QGSL Lab). It follows weekly one-hour meetings and takes the reader from their first R commands to high-performance mixed-model analysis with ASReml-R.

Who this course is for
The course is written for researchers, graduate students and undergraduates in quantitative genetics, statistics and plant and animal breeding. We assume no previous programming experience. We do assume curiosity and the willingness to type the code, make mistakes and understand them.

text:
1.1 Setting up your environment

1.1.1 What needs to be installed
We will use four tools throughout the course. Each plays a different role:



Tool
Role
Where to get it




R
The language and the interpreter that runs the code
https://cran.r-project.org


RStudio
The integrated development environment (IDE): editor, console, file and project manager
https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/


Quarto
The publishing system that turns text + code into reports, books and websites (this book is built with Quarto)
Ships with RStudio; also at https://quarto.org


Git
Version control, which records the history of every file in the project
https://git-scm.com



An important distinction: R and RStudio are not the same thing. R is the engine; RStudio is the dashboard. You can use R without RStudio (from the terminal or other editors such as VS Code or Positron), but you cannot use RStudio without R.
To check what is installed, run in the console:

R.version.string            # R version
RStudio.Version()$version   # RStudio version (only works inside RStudio)
quarto::quarto_version()    # Quarto version
system("git --version")     # Git version


R.version.string
#> [1] "R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24)"







WarningKeep R up to date



New packages often require recent versions of R. A rule of thumb for the lab: update R at least once a year, shortly after the x.y.0 release (usually in April), and reinstall your packages afterwards.




1.1.2 A tour of RStudio
When you open RStudio you will see four panes:

Editor (top left): where you write and save scripts (.R) and Quarto documents (.qmd). This is where the real work happens.
Console (bottom left): where R runs commands. Great for quick tests, terrible for keeping work, because nothing you type there is saved in an organised way.
Environment / History / Git (top right): shows the objects in the session’s memory, the command history and, once we enable Git, the state of the files.
Files / Plots / Packages / Help / Viewer (bottom right): file browser, plots, installed packages and documentation.

Two shortcuts you will use hundreds of times per lesson:







Shortcut
What it does




Ctrl + Enter (Cmd + Enter on a Mac)
Runs the current line (or selection) of the editor in the console


Ctrl + Shift + F10
Restarts the R session (we will see why this matters)

title: 1  Projects: the unit of work in R
text:
1.2 The problem: loose scripts
Imagine a lab colleague sends you this script to analyse a maize trial:

rm(list = ls())
setwd("C:/Users/joao/Desktop/phd/analyses/maize_2025")

data <- read.csv("ensaio_milho_piloto.csv")
mean(data$produtividade_t_ha)

This script looks harmless, but it has two serious problems:

setwd() with an absolute path. The path C:/Users/joao/Desktop/... only exists on João’s computer. On your computer, on the lab server, or on João’s own computer two years from now (after a reinstall), the script fails on its second line.
rm(list = ls()) gives a false sense of cleanliness. That line deletes the objects in the Environment, but it does not unload packages, does not restore options changed with options() and does not undo changes to environment variables. The script may work in your “dirty” session and fail in someone else’s.


1.2.1 The working directory
To understand the first problem we need one concept: the working directory. It is the folder from which R interprets every relative path. You can query it with getwd():

getwd()
#> [1] "/home/ana/projects/R_Course"

When you write read.csv("ensaio_milho_piloto.csv"), R looks for the file inside the working directory. If the file is somewhere else, R cannot find it. setwd() changes the working directory, which is why it looks like the solution. But it ties the script to one specific machine.
The right question is not “how do I make R find my folder?” but “how do I make sure that anyone, on any computer, can run my code without editing anything?”. The answer is the project.

title: 1  Projects: the unit of work in R
text:
1.3 The solution: RStudio projects
An RStudio project is a folder containing a .Rproj file. When you open that file (double-click it, or use File > Open Project), RStudio:

starts a fresh R session;
sets the working directory to the project folder, automatically;
keeps history, open tabs and settings separate for each project.

As a result, every path in the code can be written relative to the project root, and the same code works on any computer that has a copy of the folder.






ImportantLab rule



At the QGSL Lab, every analysis lives inside a project. A research question, a paper, a thesis or a course: each one is a project, with its own folder, its own .Rproj and its own Git repository. Loose scripts on the desktop are not accepted in code reviews.



1.3.1 Creating a project from the menu

File > New Project…
Choose New Directory > New Project.
Give it a name with no spaces and no accents (for example maize_trial_2025) and choose where the folder will be created.
Tick Create a git repository (we will use it from lesson 9 onwards).
Click Create Project.

RStudio restarts inside the new project. Notice that the project name appears in the top-right corner of the window.


1.3.2 Creating a project from code: the usethis package






NotePackage intent: usethis



Problem it solves. Project setup tasks (creating the structure, enabling Git, configuring GitHub, adding a licence, creating standard files) are repetitive and easy to get wrong by hand.
Philosophy. usethis automates these tasks with self-explanatory function names (use_git(), use_readme_md(), create_project()), always telling you what it did and what you still need to do. It belongs to the development toolchain maintained by the tidyverse team (together with devtools, roxygen2 and testthat).
Why this one and not the alternatives. The alternative is clicking through RStudio menus or creating folders and files by hand. The menu works fine for one project; usethis wins when we want to standardise dozens of lab projects and record the setup as code, which is reproducible by definition. We will return to it in lesson 9 (Git and GitHub) and in the appendix on building the lab package.


The function usethis::create_project() creates the folder, the .Rproj file and a basic .gitignore, and then opens the new project in RStudio. We will use it to create the project for the maize pilot trial. The rest of this lesson is done from inside that project, exactly as you will work on your own analyses.

text:
1.4 Hands on: the maize trial project

1.4.1 Step 1: create the project inside Documents
We will create the maize_trial_2025 project inside your Documents folder. That folder’s path changes from one operating system to another:







System
Documents folder




macOS
~/Documents (that is, /Users/your_user/Documents)


Linux Ubuntu
~/Documents, or ~/Documentos if the system was installed in Portuguese


Windows
C:/Users/your_user/Documents



In the RStudio console, run only the line for your system:

usethis::create_project("~/Documents/maize_trial_2025")                     # macOS and Linux
usethis::create_project("C:/Users/your_user/Documents/maize_trial_2025")    # Windows (replace your_user)

If you prefer, let R work out where your Documents folder is. Sys.info()[["sysname"]] returns "Darwin" on macOS, "Linux" on Linux and "Windows" on Windows; on Linux, the xdg-user-dir command reports the folder name in the system’s language:

documents_dir <- switch(
  Sys.info()[["sysname"]],
  Darwin  = "~/Documents",
  Linux   = system("xdg-user-dir DOCUMENTS", intern = TRUE),
  Windows = file.path(Sys.getenv("USERPROFILE"), "Documents")
)

usethis::create_project(file.path(documents_dir, "maize_trial_2025"))

RStudio opens a new session, already inside the project: the name maize_trial_2025 appears in the top-right corner and the Files pane shows the project folder. Any objects you had created stayed in the previous session; from now on, all code in this lesson must be typed in this new session. Check:

getwd()
#> [1] "/home/ana/Documents/maize_trial_2025"
fs::dir_tree(all = TRUE)


#> .
#> ├── .gitignore
#> ├── R
#> └── maize_trial_2025.Rproj

Notice three details:

maize_trial_2025.Rproj is the file that marks the folder as a project. Next time, just double-click it to get back to the project.
.gitignore lists files Git should ignore (for example .Rhistory and .RData).
The R/ folder is created by default; in the lab it holds reusable functions, while analyses go in scripts/.

The :: operator (as in usethis::create_project) calls a function from a package without loading the whole package with library(). We will use this form whenever a package function appears only once, because it makes explicit where the function comes from.


1.4.2 Step 2: the lab’s folder structure
Every QGSL Lab analysis follows the same structure. Still in the new project’s console, create the folders:

folders <- c(
  "data/raw",        # raw data, exactly as they came from the field or the lab
  "data/processed",  # clean data, produced by the scripts
  "scripts",         # analyses, numbered in the order they run
  "R",               # reusable functions
  "output/figures",  # generated plots
  "output/tables",   # generated tables
  "reports"          # Quarto reports
)

fs::dir_create(folders)
fs::dir_tree()


#> .
#> ├── R
#> ├── data
#> │   ├── processed
#> │   └── raw
#> ├── maize_trial_2025.Rproj
#> ├── output
#> │   ├── figures
#> │   └── tables
#> ├── reports
#> └── scripts

Notice that the paths are relative: fs::dir_create("data/raw") creates the folder inside the working directory, which is the project root. This course’s own repository follows the same structure, with a chapters/ folder instead of reports/.
Three rules give this structure its meaning:

Raw data are read-only. Never edit a file in data/raw/ by hand, not even in Excel. Every correction is made in code, which writes the result to data/processed/. That way every correction is documented and can be redone.
Everything in data/processed/ and output/ can be deleted and recreated by running the scripts. If it cannot, some step of the analysis is not in the code.
Scripts are numbered in the order they run: A01_import.R, A02_clean.R, A03_model.R. Anyone joining the project knows where to start. The letter before the number is a lab convention: a script name never starts with a number, and the A01_, A02_… prefix keeps the running order in the file listing.



1.4.3 Step 3: put the data in data/raw/
Download the pilot trial file: ensaio_milho_piloto.csv (right-click and choose Save link as if the browser opens the file instead of downloading it). The file name is Portuguese for “maize pilot trial”; the data are shared by both language versions of the book.
The browser saves the file in your downloads folder, which is not part of the project. It has to go to data/raw/. You can drag it in the file manager or, better, move it from R, in the project’s console:

file.copy(
  from = "~/Downloads/ensaio_milho_piloto.csv",   # where the browser saved it
  to = "data/raw/"                                 # into the project
)
#> [1] TRUE

list.files("data/raw")
#> [1] "ensaio_milho_piloto.csv"

On Windows, the downloads folder is C:/Users/your_user/Downloads. If file.copy() returns FALSE, the file was not found at the source path: check the name and folder with list.files("~/Downloads").

text:
1.5 File paths

1.5.1 Absolute and relative
An absolute path starts at the root of the file system and identifies the file unambiguously, but only on that machine:
/home/ana/projects/R_Course/data/raw/ensaio_milho_piloto.csv    # Linux
/Users/ana/projects/R_Course/data/raw/ensaio_milho_piloto.csv   # macOS
C:/Users/ana/projects/R_Course/data/raw/ensaio_milho_piloto.csv # Windows
A relative path describes where the file is starting from the working directory:
data/raw/ensaio_milho_piloto.csv
Inside a project, the working directory is the project root, so the relative path works on any computer.






TipAlways use the forward slash /



R accepts the forward slash / on every system, including Windows. The backslash \ has to be doubled inside strings ("C:\\Users"), because it has a special meaning there. Use / and avoid the problem altogether.




1.5.2 Building paths with file.path()
Instead of pasting text together, use file.path(), which inserts the correct separator:

file.path("data", "raw", "ensaio_milho_piloto.csv")
#> [1] "data/raw/ensaio_milho_piloto.csv"



1.5.3 The here package
One subtle problem remains. The working directory is not always the project root. When Quarto renders a report, for instance, the working directory becomes the report’s folder. If your report lives in reports/, during rendering the relative path data/raw/ensaio_milho_piloto.csv would not exist (R would look for it in reports/data/raw/).






NotePackage intent: here



Problem it solves. Building paths that always point to the same place, no matter where the code runs (console, script, Quarto document in a subfolder, server), without setwd() and without absolute paths.
Philosophy. here finds the project root by searching from the current directory up through the parent folders for files that mark a project (a .Rproj, a .git folder, a .here file, among others). The here() function returns paths starting from that root. It is deliberately tiny: it does one thing, and does it well.
Why this one and not the alternatives.

setwd(): ties the code to one computer; ruled out for the reasons above.
Plain relative paths: work in the console but break when the working directory changes (as in Quarto documents in subfolders).
rprojroot: the engine behind here, more flexible but more verbose. here offers the same robustness through a one-function interface.





1.5.4 Step 4: read the data from inside the project
In the maize_trial_2025 project console, load here:

library(here)
#> here() starts at /home/ana/Documents/maize_trial_2025

The message here() starts at ... shows which folder here recognised as the root. Always check that line when you open a new project.
To build the path to the data file, pass each piece as an argument:

data_path <- here("data", "raw", "ensaio_milho_piloto.csv")
file.exists(data_path)
#> [1] TRUE

Now we read the file. In lesson 5 we will meet the readr package and its advantages; for now we use read.csv(), which ships with R:

trial <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "ensaio_milho_piloto.csv"))

head(trial)
#>   hibrido bloco produtividade_t_ha altura_planta_cm
#> 1    HB01     1               9.54              225
#> 2    HB01     2               9.93              220
#> 3    HB01     3               8.64              201
#> 4    HB02     1               9.04              213
#> 5    HB02     2               9.00              204
#> 6    HB02     3               8.86              220

This code works the same in the console, in a script in scripts/ and in a report in reports/, on any computer that has a copy of the project. That is exactly what we wanted. (This book is also a project with the same structure, which is why the results shown here are the same ones you get in yours.)
A few quick questions for our pilot trial:

nrow(trial)                         # how many plots?
#> [1] 36
unique(trial$hibrido)               # which hybrids?
#>  [1] "HB01" "HB02" "HB03" "HB04" "HB05" "HB06" "HB07" "HB08" "HB09" "HB10"
#> [11] "HB11" "HB12"
mean(trial$produtividade_t_ha)      # mean yield (t/ha)
#> [1] 9.061111
summary(trial$altura_planta_cm)     # summary of plant height (cm)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   193.0   203.0   212.5   212.6   220.0   240.0

1.6 Failing on purpose: “cannot open file”
The most common error for R beginners is this one:

read.csv("ensaio_milho_piloto.csv")
#> Warning in file(file, "rt"): cannot open file 'ensaio_milho_piloto.csv': No
#> such file or directory
#> Error in `file()`:
#> ! cannot open the connection

Read the message carefully. It says two things:

cannot open file 'ensaio_milho_piloto.csv': R could not open a file at that path.
No such file or directory: the reason is that, starting from the current working directory, no file with that name exists.

A diagnostic routine that solves almost every case:

# 1. Where is R looking?
getwd()
#> [1] "/home/ana/Documents/maize_trial_2025"

# 2. Is the file where I think it is?
file.exists(here("data", "raw", "ensaio_milho_piloto.csv"))
#> [1] TRUE

# 3. What is actually in the folder? (typos and extensions show up here)
list.files(here("data", "raw"))
#> [1] "ensaio_milho_piloto.csv"

The file exists and is in the right place: the problem is that read.csv("ensaio_milho_piloto.csv") looked for it at the project root, not in data/raw/.
The most frequent causes, in order:

The path is relative to the wrong place (missing here() or the data/raw folder).
A typo in the name or the extension (.csv vs .CSV vs .xlsx). On Linux and macOS, upper and lower case matter.
The project is not open, and the working directory is the user’s home folder.
The file stayed in the downloads folder and was never moved to data/raw/.

1.7 Clean sessions: never save .RData
By default, when you close RStudio it asks Save workspace image to ~/.RData?. If you answer “yes”, every object in the session is saved and silently comes back next time. That looks convenient, but it is the main source of analyses that “work on my machine”: the result depends on objects that no script creates.
The lab rule is: the code is the source of truth, not the session. Every object must be recreatable by running the scripts from start to finish in a fresh session.
Set this up once and for all:

In RStudio: Tools > Global Options > General, untick Restore .RData into workspace at startup and choose Never for Save workspace to .RData on exit.
Or from code:


usethis::use_blank_slate()

And adopt the habit: before you consider an analysis finished, restart the session (Ctrl + Shift + F10) and run the whole script. If it works, it is reproducible.

text:
1.8 Organising a script
A lab script always has the same anatomy. Here is an example you can save as scripts/A01_explore_pilot.R in the maize_trial_2025 project (File > New File > R Script, then save it in the scripts/ folder):

# Initial exploration of the maize pilot trial ---------------------------------
# Author: Your Name
# Goal: check that the data are read correctly and compute basic summaries.

# Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------------
library(here)

# Data -------------------------------------------------------------------------
trial <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "ensaio_milho_piloto.csv"))

# Summaries --------------------------------------------------------------------
mean(trial$produtividade_t_ha)
tapply(trial$produtividade_t_ha, trial$hibrido, mean)


The header says what the script does and why.
Packages are loaded at the top, all together. A reader immediately knows what the script depends on.
Lines ending in ---- create navigable sections in RStudio (Ctrl + Shift + R inserts one). Use the section menu at the bottom of the editor to jump between them.
There is no setwd() and no rm(list = ls()).

text:
1.9 Under the hood

1.9.1 What is inside a .Rproj
The .Rproj file is a plain text file with the project options. Since the working directory is the project root, the file name is enough:

readLines("maize_trial_2025.Rproj")


#>  [1] "Version: 1.0"                 ""                            
#>  [3] "RestoreWorkspace: No"         "SaveWorkspace: No"           
#>  [5] "AlwaysSaveHistory: Default"   ""                            
#>  [7] "EnableCodeIndexing: Yes"      "Encoding: UTF-8"             
#>  [9] ""                             "AutoAppendNewline: Yes"      
#> [11] "StripTrailingWhitespace: Yes" "LineEndingConversion: Posix" 
#> [13] ""

RStudio uses these options (for example RestoreWorkspace: No) and creates next to it a hidden .Rproj.user/ folder with the interface state (open tabs, history). That folder is personal and never goes into Git.


1.9.2 How here finds the root
here walks up the folder tree from the working directory until it finds a project marker. The dr_here() function explains its reasoning:

here::dr_here()
#> here() starts at /home/ana/Documents/maize_trial_2025.
#> - This directory contains a file matching "[.]Rproj$" with contents matching
#>   "^Version: " in the first line
#> - Initial working directory: /home/ana/Documents/maize_trial_2025/reports
#> - Current working directory: /home/ana/Documents/maize_trial_2025/reports

In this example, dr_here() was called while rendering a report in reports/: the working directory was reports/, and here still found the root through the .Rproj. The root is determined only once, when the package is loaded. So if you switch projects, restart the session.


1.9.3 Why rm(list = ls()) is not enough

library(here)
rm(list = ls())
search()   # the "here" package is still attached to the session
#>  [1] ".GlobalEnv"        "package:here"      "package:stats"  ...

ls() only lists the objects in the global environment. Loaded packages, options and environment variables survive. The only real clean-up is restarting the session.


1.9.4 The tilde ~ and your home path
The tilde ~ is a shortcut for your home folder. path.expand() shows where it points:

path.expand("~/projects")
#> [1] "/home/ana/projects"

It is handy in the console for opening projects, but it is still a user-specific path and must not appear inside analysis scripts.

All R work in the lab happens inside a project (.Rproj), which sets the working directory automatically.
Never use setwd() or absolute paths in scripts. Use paths relative to the project root, built with here().

title: 2  R as a language
text:
2.1 The console as a calculator
The most direct way to get to know a language is to talk to it. Type in the console:

62.4 + 58.1     # addition
#> [1] 120.5
70.3 - 65.8     # subtraction
#> [1] 4.5
3 * 60          # multiplication: 3 bags of 60 kg
#> [1] 180
180 / 1000      # division: kg to tonnes
#> [1] 0.18
2^10            # power
#> [1] 1024

Two lesser-known operators show up often when arranging plots into blocks and rows:

17 %/% 5   # integer division: how many full blocks of 5 plots fit in 17?
#> [1] 3
17 %% 5    # remainder: how many plots are left over?
#> [1] 2

The order of operations follows mathematics: powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. When in doubt, use parentheses; they also make the code easier to read.

2 + 3 * 4
#> [1] 14
(2 + 3) * 4
#> [1] 20
-2^2      # careful: the power comes before the minus sign
#> [1] -4
(-2)^2
#> [1] 4

Very large or very small numbers are shown in scientific notation, and you can type them that way:

1.5e6     # 1.5 million plants per hectare? Check the density!
#> [1] 1500000
2.3e-4    # a rare allele frequency
#> [1] 0.00023







WarningDecimal point, not comma



In R the decimal separator is always the point. 62,4 is not a number: the comma separates function arguments. In lesson 5 we will see how to read spreadsheets that use a decimal comma, as Brazilian ones do, without editing them.



2.1.1 Why 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
#> [1] FALSE

This is not an R bug. Computers store decimal numbers in base 2, and fractions such as 0.1 have no exact binary representation, just as 1/3 has no exact decimal one. The stored value is very close to 0.1, but not identical:

print(0.1 + 0.2, digits = 17)
#> [1] 0.30000000000000004
print(0.3, digits = 17)
#> [1] 0.29999999999999999

The difference is tiny, but enough for == to answer FALSE. To compare decimal numbers, use a tolerance:

all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)
#> [1] TRUE
isTRUE(all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))   # the safe form to use inside an if
#> [1] TRUE

This matters in practice: when checking that the allele frequencies at a locus add up to 1, or that a relationship matrix is symmetric, compare with a tolerance, never with ==.

title: 2  R as a language
text:
2.2 Objects and assignment
Results that vanish in the console are not much use. To keep them, we create objects with the assignment operator <-:

bag_weight_kg <- 60
yield_bags_ha <- 62.4

yield_bags_ha * bag_weight_kg / 1000   # t/ha
#> [1] 3.744

Read <- as “gets”: bag_weight_kg gets 60. In RStudio, the shortcut Alt + - inserts the operator with the right spacing.






Tip<- or =?



Both work for top-level assignment, but the lab style (and that of most of the community) is to use <- to assign and keep = for function arguments, as in round(x, digits = 2). Code is easier to read when each symbol has a single role.



2.2.1 Rules and style for names
R accepts names made of letters, numbers, . and _, as long as they do not start with a number or _. It is case-sensitive: Yield and yield are different objects.
The lab style:

snake_case: lower-case words separated by _ (yield_bags_ha, n_plots).
Descriptive names and, where relevant, with the unit (height_cm, days_to_maturity). Six months from now you will not remember whether ht was in cm or m.
No accented characters in object or file names. They work on most systems, but cause encoding problems when code moves between computers.


2a <- 10           # invalid: starts with a number
#> Error in parse(text = input): <text>:1:2: unexpected symbol
#> 1: 2a
#>      ^


yield_bags_ha
#> [1] 62.4
Yield_bags_ha   # a different name: R cannot find it
#> Error:
#> ! object 'Yield_bags_ha' not found

The message object 'Yield_bags_ha' not found is by far the most common one in daily work. Most of the time it is a typo or an object that has not yet been created in this session.


2.2.2 What assignment really does
Consider:

x <- 10
y <- x
x <- 20
y
#> [1] 10

y is still 10. The assignment y <- x does not create a “shortcut” to x; when x changes, R creates a new value and y keeps pointing at the old one. This rule (called copy-on-modify) makes R predictable: changing one object never changes another unless you ask it to.

title: 2  R as a language
text:
2.3 Everything is a vector
There is no such thing as a “lone number” in R. The 62.4 we typed is a vector of length 1. Longer vectors are created with c() (for combine):

yield_bags_ha <- c(62.4, 58.1, 70.3, 66.0, 65.8)
length(yield_bags_ha)
#> [1] 5

The big advantage is that operations are vectorised: they apply to every element at once, without you having to write a loop.

yield_t_ha <- yield_bags_ha * bag_weight_kg / 1000
yield_t_ha
#> [1] 3.744 3.486 4.218 3.960 3.948

mean(yield_t_ha)
#> [1] 3.8712
max(yield_t_ha)
#> [1] 4.218
yield_t_ha > 3.9    # which plots went above 3.9 t/ha?
#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE


2.3.1 The recycling rule
When two vectors of different lengths enter the same operation, the shorter one is repeated until it matches the longer:

c(1, 2, 3, 4) * c(10, 100)
#> [1]  10 200  30 400

This is useful (multiplying by a single number is recycling a vector of length 1), but also dangerous. If the longer length is not a multiple of the shorter, R warns you:

c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5) * c(10, 100)
#> Warning in c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5) * c(10, 100): longer object length is not a
#> multiple of shorter object length
#> [1]  10 200  30 400  50

This warning almost always signals a logic error, such as data missing from one block. Take it seriously.

title: 2  R as a language
text:
2.4 Atomic types
Every vector has a type, and all its elements share that type. The four you will use all the time:



Type
Example in the trial
How to write it




logical
did the plot lodge?
TRUE, FALSE


integer
days to maturity
118L (the L marks an integer)


double
yield in bags/ha
62.4, 60


character
cultivar name
"SJ-04" (in quotes)




lodging <- c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
days_to_maturity <- c(118L, 121L, 125L, 119L, 123L)
cultivar <- c("SJ-01", "SJ-02", "SJ-03", "SJ-04", "SJ-05")

typeof(lodging)
#> [1] "logical"
typeof(days_to_maturity)
#> [1] "integer"
typeof(yield_bags_ha)
#> [1] "double"
typeof(cultivar)
#> [1] "character"

Notice that 60 is a double, not an integer. In R, numbers typed without the L suffix are always double. Together the two types form what R calls numeric:

typeof(60)
#> [1] "double"
typeof(60L)
#> [1] "integer"
is.numeric(60L)
#> [1] TRUE

There are also the complex and raw types, which rarely show up in breeding analyses.

section: 2.5 Coercion: when R changes the type
text:
2.5 Coercion: when R changes the type
Since a vector can only have one type, what happens when we mix types?

c(62.4, "SJ-01")
#> [1] "62.4"  "SJ-01"
c(TRUE, 2L)
#> [1] 1 2
c(1L, 2.5)
#> [1] 1.0 2.5

R converts everything to the most flexible type, following this hierarchy:
logical → integer → double → character
This is called implicit coercion. It has a very practical use: in numeric operations, TRUE becomes 1 and FALSE becomes 0. So counting and computing proportions of logical conditions is trivial:

sum(lodging)     # how many plots lodged?
#> [1] 2
mean(lodging)    # what proportion lodged?
#> [1] 0.4
sum(yield_bags_ha > 65)
#> [1] 3


2.5.1 Explicit coercion and the comma trap
The as.*() functions convert types on purpose:

as.character(days_to_maturity)
#> [1] "118" "121" "125" "119" "123"
as.integer("118")
#> [1] 118
as.integer(3.9)       # truncates, does not round!
#> [1] 3
round(3.9)
#> [1] 4

When the conversion is impossible, the result is NA with a warning. The classic case in Brazil is a number typed with a decimal comma:

as.numeric("62,4")
#> Warning: NAs introduced by coercion
#> [1] NA

The warning NAs introduced by coercion means “there was text that did not look like a number, and I replaced it with NA”. An immediate fix is to swap the comma for a point before converting:

as.numeric(sub(",", ".", "62,4"))
#> [1] 62.4

In lesson 5 we will solve this at import time, telling R about the Brazilian format, without touching the values one by one.






ImportantA column of numbers that “turned into” text



If a single cell of a yield column contains "62,4", "lost" or "-", the whole column is read as character, and mean() stops working. When a numeric calculation fails, the first question is: what is the type of this vector? typeof() and str() answer it.

text:
2.6 Special values

2.6.1 NA: the missing value
NA (not available) represents a value that should exist but was not observed: a plot lost to hail, a plant that never flowered. It is contagious, and rightly so: if a value is unknown, any calculation involving it is unknown too.

yield_bags_ha <- c(62.4, 58.1, NA, 66.0, 65.8)

yield_bags_ha * 2
#> [1] 124.8 116.2    NA 132.0 131.6
mean(yield_bags_ha)
#> [1] NA

Most summary functions have an na.rm (NA remove) argument:

mean(yield_bags_ha, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 63.075

Use na.rm = TRUE deliberately: the mean is now over 4 plots, not 5. In a trial, that can unbalance the comparison between cultivars.
To find the missing values, use is.na(), never == NA:

yield_bags_ha == NA      # always NA: "is it equal to an unknown value?"
#> [1] NA NA NA NA NA
is.na(yield_bags_ha)
#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE
sum(is.na(yield_bags_ha))
#> [1] 1
which(is.na(yield_bags_ha))
#> [1] 3

NA has a type too. Most of the time this is invisible, but there are specific versions for when the type needs to be explicit:

typeof(NA)
#> [1] "logical"
typeof(NA_real_)
#> [1] "double"
typeof(NA_character_)
#> [1] "character"



2.6.2 NULL: the absence of an object
NULL is not a missing value: it is the absence of anything. It has length zero and disappears when combined:

length(NULL)
#> [1] 0
length(NA)
#> [1] 1
c(62.4, NULL, 58.1)
#> [1] 62.4 58.1
c(62.4, NA, 58.1)
#> [1] 62.4   NA 58.1

You will meet NULL as the result of functions that “returned nothing” and as the default value of optional arguments.


2.6.3 NaN and Inf: impossible or infinite results

0 / 0          # NaN: "not a number"
#> [1] NaN
1 / 0          # Inf
#> [1] Inf
log(0)         # -Inf
#> [1] -Inf
sqrt(-1)       # NaN, with a warning
#> Warning in sqrt(-1): NaNs produced
#> [1] NaN

NaN tends to appear when computing something like a variance from a single observation, or a ratio of zeros, for example a harvest index for a plot with no plants. To filter all these cases at once:

values <- c(1.2, NA, NaN, Inf, -Inf, 3.4)
is.na(values)       # NA and NaN
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE
is.nan(values)      # only NaN
#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE
is.finite(values)   # only the "ordinary" numbers
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE




Value
Meaning
Length
Test




NA
exists, but is unknown
1
is.na()


NULL
does not exist
0
is.null()


NaN
undefined mathematical result
1
is.nan()


Inf, -Inf
infinity
1
is.infinite()

text:
2.7 Functions
Almost everything you do in R is calling functions. A call is the function name followed by parentheses holding the arguments:

round(66.04167, digits = 1)
#> [1] 66


2.7.1 Positional and named arguments
Arguments can be passed by position or by name. The two calls below are equivalent:

round(66.04167, 1)
#> [1] 66
round(digits = 1, x = 66.04167)
#> [1] 66

The lab rule of thumb: the first argument (usually the data) goes by position; the rest go by name. round(x, digits = 1) is clearer than round(x, 1), especially in functions with many arguments.
To see a function’s arguments and their default values:

args(round)
#> function (x, digits = 0, ...) 
#> NULL
args(seq)
#> function (...) 
#> NULL

The digits = 0 in round is a default value: if you do not supply it, it is used.

seq(from = 1, to = 25, by = 6)   # plot numbers every 6
#> [1]  1  7 13 19 25
seq_len(5)                       # 1 to 5, the safe way to create indices
#> [1] 1 2 3 4 5
rep(c("B1", "B2", "B3"), times = 2)
#> [1] "B1" "B2" "B3" "B1" "B2" "B3"
rep(c("B1", "B2", "B3"), each = 2)
#> [1] "B1" "B1" "B2" "B2" "B3" "B3"



2.7.2 Writing your first function
If you convert bags to tonnes more than twice, it is time to write a function:

bags_to_t <- function(bags, bag_weight_kg = 60) {
  bags * bag_weight_kg / 1000
}

bags_to_t(62.4)
#> [1] 3.744
bags_to_t(yield_bags_ha)
#> [1] 3.744 3.486    NA 3.960 3.948
bags_to_t(150, bag_weight_kg = 50)  # 50 kg bags
#> [1] 7.5

A function has three parts: the arguments (bags, and bag_weight_kg with default 60), the body between braces and the return value, which is the result of the last expression in the body. Because we only used vectorised operations, the function already works for a single value or a whole vector. In lesson 13 we will return to functions with input validation and custom error messages.

text:
2.8 Getting help
Every R function has a documentation page:

?mean              # help for a function
help("mean")       # the same
??"standard deviation"   # topic search across all installed packages
example(mean)      # runs the examples from the help page

A help page always has the same sections. Read them in this order:

Usage: how to call the function and which arguments have defaults.
Arguments: what each argument accepts.
Value: what the function returns (type and structure).
Examples: the fastest way to understand the function. Copy, run and modify.

When the documentation is not enough, search for the exact error message, in quotes, in a search engine or on Posit Community. Very often someone has already had the same problem.

section: 2.9 How to read an error message
text:
2.9 How to read an error message
R communicates through three kinds of condition, in increasing order of severity:



Condition
What it means
Does the code continue?




message
information
yes


warning
something looks off, but there is a result
yes


error
impossible to continue
no



In the console, an error almost always looks like Error in <call> : <reason>, or simply Error: <reason> when the failure happens at the top level. The call tells you where it happened and the reason tells you why.
In this book, messages appear in a two-line format, the same one used by tidyverse packages: the first line says where (Error in ...) and the second, starting with !, says why. You read it the same way. Here are the most common errors:

"62.4" + 1
#> Error in `"62.4" + 1`:
#> ! non-numeric argument to binary operator

non-numeric argument to binary operator: one side of + is text. Ask typeof() about each side.

average(yield_bags_ha)
#> Error in `average()`:
#> ! could not find function "average"

could not find function "average": no function exists with that name (it is mean), or it belongs to a package that has not been loaded.

mean(cultivar)
#> Warning in mean.default(cultivar): argument is not numeric or logical:
#> returning NA
#> [1] NA

There was no error here, but a warning: mean() received text and returned NA. Warnings like this are worse than errors, because the code carries on with a meaningless result.

round(62.4, digits = 1
#> Error in parse(text = input): <text>:2:0: unexpected end of input
#> 1: round(62.4, digits = 1
#>    ^

Syntax errors (a parenthesis that never closes, an extra comma) appear before the code runs. In the console, an open parenthesis turns the prompt from > into +, waiting for the rest of the command; press Esc to cancel.
The tidyverse packages, which we will use from lesson 4 onwards, add to the two-line format further lines starting with ℹ or ✖, which give context and often suggest the fix. It pays to read them to the end.






TipA routine for any error




Read the whole message, slowly, ideally out loud.
Identify which call failed and which object is involved.
Inspect that object: typeof(), length(), str(), head().
Shrink the problem: run only the failing line, with a minimal example.
Only then search for the message online.

text:
2.10 Under the hood

2.10.1 Everything is a function call
Even operators are functions. 2 + 3 is a convenient way of writing a call to the function `+`:

`+`(2, 3)
#> [1] 5
`[`(cultivar, 2)
#> [1] "SJ-02"

That explains why the error from "62.4" + 1 talks about a binary operator: the + function received two arguments (it is binary) and one of them was not numeric.


2.10.2 Integers have a limit
Integers take 32 bits, so there is a largest possible integer:

.Machine$integer.max
#> [1] 2147483647
.Machine$integer.max + 1L
#> Warning in .Machine$integer.max + 1L: NAs produced by integer overflow
#> [1] NA

The result is NA with an overflow warning. This can happen when multiplying large counts (number of markers × number of individuals). double has no such problem at the same scale, which is why R uses double by default.


2.10.3 Attributes
Vectors can carry attributes, metadata that do not change the values. The most common one is names:

names(yield_bags_ha) <- cultivar
yield_bags_ha
#> SJ-01 SJ-02 SJ-03 SJ-04 SJ-05 
#>  62.4  58.1    NA  66.0  65.8
yield_bags_ha["SJ-04"]
#> SJ-04 
#>    66
attributes(yield_bags_ha)
#> $names
#> [1] "SJ-01" "SJ-02" "SJ-03" "SJ-04" "SJ-05"

Factors, matrices and data frames, which we will meet in the next lesson, are vectors with special attributes. Understanding this demystifies much of R’s behaviour.

text:
2.11 Exercises

Unit conversion. A soybean trial yielded c(55.2, 61.7, 48.9, 72.1) bags per hectare. Convert to kg/ha and to t/ha, and compute the mean in t/ha rounded to two decimal places.







TipSolution






bags_ha <- c(55.2, 61.7, 48.9, 72.1)
kg_ha <- bags_ha * 60
t_ha <- kg_ha / 1000
kg_ha
#> [1] 3312 3702 2934 4326
round(mean(t_ha), digits = 2)
#> [1] 3.57





Predicting types. Without running the code, predict the type of each vector. Then check with typeof().


c(1, TRUE, FALSE)
c("1", 2, 3)
c(1L, NA)
c(1.5, NA, 3L)







TipSolution






typeof(c(1, TRUE, FALSE))   # double: the logical is promoted to double
#> [1] "double"
typeof(c("1", 2, 3))        # character: one string pulls everything to text
#> [1] "character"
typeof(c(1L, NA))           # integer: NA adapts to its neighbours' type
#> [1] "integer"
typeof(c(1.5, NA, 3L))      # double
#> [1] "double"





Missing values. For height_cm <- c(98, 102, NA, 95, NA, 110), compute: the number of plants measured, the mean height of the measured plants and the positions of the plants without a measurement.







TipSolution






height_cm <- c(98, 102, NA, 95, NA, 110)
sum(!is.na(height_cm))
#> [1] 4
mean(height_cm, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 101.25
which(is.na(height_cm))
#> [1] 3 5

The ! operator negates logical values: !is.na() means “is not missing”.




The comma spreadsheet. You received the vector weight_100_seeds <- c("15,2", "16,8", "14,9", "-", "17,1"). Convert it to numbers so that "-" becomes NA, and compute the mean. Why does a warning appear, and why is it acceptable here?







TipSolution






weight_100_seeds <- c("15,2", "16,8", "14,9", "-", "17,1")
weight_num <- as.numeric(sub(",", ".", weight_100_seeds))
#> Warning: NAs introduced by coercion
weight_num
#> [1] 15.2 16.8 14.9   NA 17.1
mean(weight_num, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 16

The warning NAs introduced by coercion appears because "-" cannot be converted. It is acceptable because we know "-" was how the spreadsheet marked a lost sample. In production code, make this explicit by replacing "-" with NA before converting; that way an unexpected warning will still catch your attention.




Your own function. Write a function kg_ha_to_bags(kg, bag_weight_kg = 60) that does the reverse of bags_to_t(), starting from kg/ha. Test it with c(3600, 4200) and with 50 kg bags.







TipSolution






kg_ha_to_bags <- function(kg, bag_weight_kg = 60) {
  kg / bag_weight_kg
}

kg_ha_to_bags(c(3600, 4200))
#> [1] 60 70
kg_ha_to_bags(c(3600, 4200), bag_weight_kg = 50)
#> [1] 72 84

Use <- to assign and = for arguments; names in snake_case, descriptive and with units.

title: 3  Data structures
text:
3.1 The map of structures
In the previous lesson we saw that every piece of data in R lives inside a vector of a single type. The structures in this lesson are ways of organising those vectors. Two questions decide which one to use:




All elements of the same type
Elements of different types




One dimension
atomic vector
list


Two dimensions
matrix
data.frame / tibble



A SNP genotype matrix (all numbers 0, 1 or 2) is homogeneous and two-dimensional: a matrix. A trial spreadsheet with cultivar (text), block (integer) and yield (decimal) is heterogeneous and two-dimensional: a data.frame. The output of a model, with coefficients, residuals and the formula used, is heterogeneous and free-form: a list.

3  Data structures

title: 3  Data structures
text:
3.2 Vectors: selecting elements
We will use the yield of six soybean cultivars in bags per hectare:

yield <- c(62.4, 58.1, 70.3, 66.0, 65.8, 54.9)
names(yield) <- c("SJ-01", "SJ-02", "SJ-03", "SJ-04", "SJ-05", "SJ-06")
yield
#> SJ-01 SJ-02 SJ-03 SJ-04 SJ-05 SJ-06 
#>  62.4  58.1  70.3  66.0  65.8  54.9

The [ operator selects elements. There are four ways of saying which ones:

# 1. By position (R starts counting at 1, not 0)
yield[3]
#> SJ-03 
#>  70.3
yield[c(1, 3, 5)]
#> SJ-01 SJ-03 SJ-05 
#>  62.4  70.3  65.8
yield[2:4]
#> SJ-02 SJ-03 SJ-04 
#>  58.1  70.3  66.0

# 2. By exclusion: negative indices drop elements
yield[-1]
#> SJ-02 SJ-03 SJ-04 SJ-05 SJ-06 
#>  58.1  70.3  66.0  65.8  54.9
yield[-c(1, 2)]
#> SJ-03 SJ-04 SJ-05 SJ-06 
#>  70.3  66.0  65.8  54.9

# 3. By name
yield["SJ-04"]
#> SJ-04 
#>    66
yield[c("SJ-01", "SJ-06")]
#> SJ-01 SJ-06 
#>  62.4  54.9

# 4. By logical condition: the logical vector acts as a filter
yield[yield > 65]
#> SJ-03 SJ-04 SJ-05 
#>  70.3  66.0  65.8

The fourth form is the most powerful and the one you will use most. It helps to see what happens in two steps:

yield > 65          # first, a logical vector of the same length
#> SJ-01 SJ-02 SJ-03 SJ-04 SJ-05 SJ-06 
#> FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE
yield[yield > 65]   # then only the TRUE positions are kept
#> SJ-03 SJ-04 SJ-05 
#>  70.3  66.0  65.8

Conditions can be combined with & (and), | (or) and ! (not):

yield[yield > 60 & yield < 68]
#> SJ-01 SJ-04 SJ-05 
#>  62.4  66.0  65.8
yield[!(names(yield) %in% c("SJ-01", "SJ-02"))]
#> SJ-03 SJ-04 SJ-05 SJ-06 
#>  70.3  66.0  65.8  54.9

The %in% operator asks “is this element in this set?” and is indispensable for filtering lists of cultivars or markers.
To know where the elements meeting a condition are, use which():

which(yield > 65)
#> SJ-03 SJ-04 SJ-05 
#>     3     4     5
which.max(yield)
#> SJ-03 
#>     3


3.2.1 Going out of bounds

yield[10]
#> <NA> 
#>   NA

Asking for a position that does not exist does not raise an error: it returns NA. This silent behaviour is a good reason to check length() before indexing by position.


3.2.2 Modifying elements
The same syntax replaces values:

yield["SJ-02"] <- 59.0
yield[yield < 56] <- NA   # flag a suspicious value as missing
yield
#> SJ-01 SJ-02 SJ-03 SJ-04 SJ-05 SJ-06 
#>  62.4  59.0  70.3  66.0  65.8    NA

title: 3  Data structures
text:
3.3 Factors: categorical variables
Block, location, cultivar and resistance class are categories, not free text. R has a dedicated structure for them, the factor:

block <- factor(c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3))
block
#> [1] 1 2 3 1 2 3 1 2 3
#> Levels: 1 2 3
levels(block)
#> [1] "1" "2" "3"
nlevels(block)
#> [1] 3
table(block)
#> block
#> 1 2 3 
#> 3 3 3

A factor stores two things: the levels (the possible categories) and, for each observation, which level it belongs to. That brings three advantages:

Statistical models treat factors as categories. If block were numeric, lm() would estimate a slope for “block”, which makes no sense. As a factor, it estimates one effect per block.
The levels set the order in tables and plots.
Levels with no observations still exist, which is useful to show that a category ended up empty.


3.3.1 Level order and ordered factors
By default, levels are sorted alphabetically. When the order is meaningful, specify it:

reaction <- c("susceptible", "resistant", "moderate", "resistant", "susceptible")

factor(reaction)   # alphabetical: moderate, resistant, susceptible
#> [1] susceptible resistant   moderate    resistant   susceptible
#> Levels: moderate resistant susceptible

reaction_f <- factor(
  reaction,
  levels = c("resistant", "moderate", "susceptible"),
  ordered = TRUE
)
reaction_f
#> [1] susceptible resistant   moderate    resistant   susceptible
#> Levels: resistant < moderate < susceptible
reaction_f < "susceptible"   # comparisons only make sense for ordered factors
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE

Values that are not among the levels become NA, with no error. Watch out for typos:

factor(c("resistant", "Resistant"), levels = c("resistant", "moderate", "susceptible"))
#> [1] resistant <NA>     
#> Levels: resistant moderate susceptible



3.3.2 The trap: turning a factor into a number
Internally, a factor is a vector of integers with a label for each integer. This leads to one of the most treacherous errors in R:

dose_kg_ha <- factor(c("60", "90", "120", "60", "120"))
as.numeric(dose_kg_ha)     # wrong! these are the internal level codes
#> [1] 2 3 1 2 1

The levels are in alphabetical order ("120", "60", "90"), so R returned 1, 2 and 3 instead of the doses. The correct way goes through text:

as.numeric(as.character(dose_kg_ha))
#> [1]  60  90 120  60 120

In lesson 8 we will meet the forcats package, which makes working with factors (reordering, renaming, lumping levels) much clearer.

title: 3  Data structures
text:
3.4 Matrices
A matrix is an atomic vector arranged in rows and columns. The classic example in genetics is the marker matrix: each row an individual, each column a SNP, and each cell the number of copies of the reference allele (0, 1 or 2).

markers <- matrix(
  c(0, 1, 2, 1, 0,
    1, 1, 2, 0, 0,
    2, 1, 1, 0, 1,
    0, 2, 2, 1, 0),
  nrow = 4,
  byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(
    c("HB01", "HB02", "HB03", "HB04"),
    c("snp1", "snp2", "snp3", "snp4", "snp5")
  )
)
markers
#>      snp1 snp2 snp3 snp4 snp5
#> HB01    0    1    2    1    0
#> HB02    1    1    2    0    0
#> HB03    2    1    1    0    1
#> HB04    0    2    2    1    0
dim(markers)
#> [1] 4 5

The byrow = TRUE argument fills the matrix row by row, the order in which we typed the values. Without it, R would fill it column by column.
Indexing uses [row, column]; leaving a position empty means “all”:

markers["HB02", ]          # every SNP for HB02
#> snp1 snp2 snp3 snp4 snp5 
#>    1    1    2    0    0
markers[, "snp3"]          # snp3 for every hybrid
#> HB01 HB02 HB03 HB04 
#>    2    2    1    2
markers[1:2, c("snp1", "snp5")]
#>      snp1 snp5
#> HB01    0    0
#> HB02    1    0

Arithmetic is still vectorised, and there are dedicated functions for rows and columns:

# Reference allele frequency at each SNP
colMeans(markers) / 2
#>  snp1  snp2  snp3  snp4  snp5 
#> 0.375 0.625 0.875 0.250 0.125

# Number of heterozygous loci (value 1) in each hybrid
rowSums(markers == 1)
#> HB01 HB02 HB03 HB04 
#>    2    2    3    1


3.4.1 The silent drop
When you select a single column, the matrix “collapses” into a vector:

markers[, "snp3"]
#> HB01 HB02 HB03 HB04 
#>    2    2    1    2
markers[, "snp3", drop = FALSE]
#>      snp3
#> HB01    2
#> HB02    2
#> HB03    1
#> HB04    2

When you write a function that must always receive a matrix, use drop = FALSE. This behaviour is a common source of bugs in genetics code, when a quality filter happens to leave a single marker.
We will return to matrices in depth in lesson 27 (matrix algebra) and in Module 5 (relationship matrices). To go beyond two dimensions there are arrays (array()), useful, for example, to store one marker matrix per chromosome.

title: 3  Data structures
text:
3.5 Lists
A list is a vector in which each element can be anything: a number, a string, a vector, a matrix, another list. It is R’s most flexible structure:

trial <- list(
  name = "Soybean cultivar trial",
  locations = c("Viçosa", "Rio Verde"),
  n_blocks = 4L,
  markers = markers
)
str(trial)
#> List of 4
#>  $ name     : chr "Soybean cultivar trial"
#>  $ locations: chr [1:2] "Viçosa" "Rio Verde"
#>  $ n_blocks : int 4
#>  $ markers  : num [1:4, 1:5] 0 1 2 0 1 1 1 2 2 2 ...
#>   ..- attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2
#>   .. ..$ : chr [1:4] "HB01" "HB02" "HB03" "HB04"
#>   .. ..$ : chr [1:5] "snp1" "snp2" "snp3" "snp4" ...

str() (for structure) is the best way to look at a list: it shows the name, the type and the start of the content of each element.

3.5.1 [, [[ and $
This is the most important distinction in the lesson. Think of the list as a sample box with labelled compartments:

[ returns a smaller box, still a list, containing the chosen compartments.
[[ opens the compartment and returns its contents.
$ is a shortcut for [[ with the name written directly.


trial["locations"]        # a list with one element
#> $locations
#> [1] "Viçosa"    "Rio Verde"
class(trial["locations"])
#> [1] "list"

trial[["locations"]]      # the character vector itself
#> [1] "Viçosa"    "Rio Verde"
class(trial[["locations"]])
#> [1] "character"

trial$locations           # the same as trial[["locations"]]
#> [1] "Viçosa"    "Rio Verde"

The difference shows up when you try to use the result:

length(trial["locations"])     # 1: the "box" has one compartment
#> [1] 1
length(trial[["locations"]])   # 2: the vector has two locations
#> [1] 2
trial["n_blocks"] * 2          # error: you cannot multiply a list
#> Error in `trial["n_blocks"] * 2`:
#> ! non-numeric argument to binary operator
trial[["n_blocks"]] * 2
#> [1] 8

You can also chain selections to reach something inside an element:

trial$locations[2]
#> [1] "Rio Verde"
trial$markers["HB03", "snp1"]
#> [1] 2



3.5.2 Why lists matter
You will rarely build complex lists by hand, but you will receive them all the time. Almost every modelling function returns a list:

model <- lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars)
typeof(model)
#> [1] "list"
names(model)
#>  [1] "coefficients"  "residuals"     "effects"       "rank"         
#>  [5] "fitted.values" "assign"        "qr"            "df.residual"  
#>  [9] "xlevels"       "call"          "terms"         "model"
model$coefficients
#> (Intercept)       speed 
#>  -17.579095    3.932409

In Module 2, the purrr package will make lists a central tool: we will fit one model per environment and keep them all in a list.

title: 3  Data structures
text:
3.6 Tables: data.frame
A data.frame is the structure of spreadsheets: each column is a vector (with its own type) and all columns have the same length.

soy <- data.frame(
  cultivar = c("SJ-01", "SJ-02", "SJ-03", "SJ-04"),
  block = factor(c(1, 1, 2, 2)),
  yield_bags_ha = c(62.4, 58.1, 70.3, 66.0),
  lodging = c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
)
soy
#>   cultivar block yield_bags_ha lodging
#> 1    SJ-01     1          62.4   FALSE
#> 2    SJ-02     1          58.1   FALSE
#> 3    SJ-03     2          70.3    TRUE
#> 4    SJ-04     2          66.0   FALSE

Inspection functions you will use on every new dataset:

str(soy)
#> 'data.frame':    4 obs. of  4 variables:
#>  $ cultivar     : chr  "SJ-01" "SJ-02" "SJ-03" "SJ-04"
#>  $ block        : Factor w/ 2 levels "1","2": 1 1 2 2
#>  $ yield_bags_ha: num  62.4 58.1 70.3 66
#>  $ lodging      : logi  FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE
nrow(soy)
#> [1] 4
ncol(soy)
#> [1] 4
names(soy)
#> [1] "cultivar"      "block"         "yield_bags_ha" "lodging"
summary(soy)
#>       cultivar block yield_bags_ha    lodging       
#>  Length   :4   1:2   Min.   :58.10   Mode :logical  
#>  N.unique :4   2:2   1st Qu.:61.33   FALSE:3        
#>  N.blank  :0         Median :64.20   TRUE :1        
#>  Min.nchar:5         Mean   :64.20                  
#>  Max.nchar:5         3rd Qu.:67.08                  
#>                      Max.   :70.30

Indexing combines what we saw for matrices and lists:

soy$yield_bags_ha                     # one column, as a vector
#> [1] 62.4 58.1 70.3 66.0
soy[["cultivar"]]                     # likewise
#> [1] "SJ-01" "SJ-02" "SJ-03" "SJ-04"
soy[soy$yield_bags_ha > 60, ]         # rows meeting a condition
#>   cultivar block yield_bags_ha lodging
#> 1    SJ-01     1          62.4   FALSE
#> 3    SJ-03     2          70.3    TRUE
#> 4    SJ-04     2          66.0   FALSE
soy[, c("cultivar", "lodging")]       # some columns
#>   cultivar lodging
#> 1    SJ-01   FALSE
#> 2    SJ-02   FALSE
#> 3    SJ-03    TRUE
#> 4    SJ-04   FALSE
soy$yield_t_ha <- soy$yield_bags_ha * 60 / 1000  # new column
soy
#>   cultivar block yield_bags_ha lodging yield_t_ha
#> 1    SJ-01     1          62.4   FALSE      3.744
#> 2    SJ-02     1          58.1   FALSE      3.486
#> 3    SJ-03     2          70.3    TRUE      4.218
#> 4    SJ-04     2          66.0   FALSE      3.960

From lesson 6 onwards we will do these operations with dplyr, which is more readable. But it is important to know the base form: you will find it in older code, inside packages and in answers online.

3.6.1 The data.frame gotchas
data.frame has behaviours inherited from decades ago that surprise newcomers:

soy[, "cultivar"]       # selected one column... and returned a vector, not a table
#> [1] "SJ-01" "SJ-02" "SJ-03" "SJ-04"
soy$lodg                # completed "lodg" to "lodging" without warning!
#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

The second case, called partial matching, is dangerous: if you mistype a column name, R may return another column without saying anything.

title: 3  Data structures
text:
3.7 Modern tables: tibble






NotePackage intent: tibble



Problem it solves. The surprising behaviours of data.frame (silent conversion to a vector, partial matching, printing thousands of rows in the console) let bugs slip through unnoticed.
Philosophy. A tibble is a more cautious data.frame: it does fewer things on its own and warns you earlier when something looks wrong. It does not change types, does not complete names, does not create row names and prints only what fits on screen, showing the type of each column.
Why this one and not the alternatives. A tibble is still a data.frame: any function that accepts a data.frame accepts a tibble. We gain safety without losing compatibility. It is also the format returned by every tidyverse package (readr, dplyr, tidyr), so adopting it now avoids converting back and forth. The data.table alternative is excellent for very large data and will be covered in lesson 18, but it has its own syntax that we prefer to introduce later.



library(tibble)

soy_tb <- tibble(
  cultivar = c("SJ-01", "SJ-02", "SJ-03", "SJ-04"),
  block = factor(c(1, 1, 2, 2)),
  yield_bags_ha = c(62.4, 58.1, 70.3, 66.0),
  yield_t_ha = yield_bags_ha * 60 / 1000   # uses a column just created
)
soy_tb
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   cultivar block yield_bags_ha yield_t_ha
#>   <chr>    <fct>         <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 SJ-01    1              62.4       3.74
#> 2 SJ-02    1              58.1       3.49
#> 3 SJ-03    2              70.3       4.22
#> 4 SJ-04    2              66         3.96

Look at the printout: the dimensions (4 × 4) and, under each name, the column type (<chr>, <fct>, <dbl>). Compare the gotchas:

soy_tb[, "cultivar"]    # still a tibble
#> # A tibble: 4 × 1
#>   cultivar
#>   <chr>   
#> 1 SJ-01   
#> 2 SJ-02   
#> 3 SJ-03   
#> 4 SJ-04
soy_tb$yield            # NULL and a warning, instead of guessing the column
#> Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: `yield`.
#> NULL

To type small tables in code, tribble() lets you write row by row, which is much more readable:

locations <- tribble(
  ~location,     ~state, ~altitude_m,
  "Viçosa",      "MG",   650,
  "Rio Verde",   "GO",   750,
  "Londrina",    "PR",   585
)
locations
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   location  state altitude_m
#>   <chr>     <chr>      <dbl>
#> 1 Viçosa    MG           650
#> 2 Rio Verde GO           750
#> 3 Londrina  PR           585

And as_tibble() converts an existing data.frame:

as_tibble(soy)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   cultivar block yield_bags_ha lodging yield_t_ha
#>   <chr>    <fct>         <dbl> <lgl>        <dbl>
#> 1 SJ-01    1              62.4 FALSE         3.74
#> 2 SJ-02    1              58.1 FALSE         3.49
#> 3 SJ-03    2              70.3 TRUE          4.22
#> 4 SJ-04    2              66   FALSE         3.96

text:
3.8 Under the hood

3.8.1 A data.frame is a list

typeof(soy)
#> [1] "list"
is.list(soy)
#> [1] TRUE
length(soy)     # the number of columns!
#> [1] 5

A data.frame is a list of vectors of equal length, with the attributes names, row.names and class. That is why soy[["cultivar"]] and soy$cultivar work: they are list operations.

attributes(soy)
#> $names
#> [1] "cultivar"      "block"         "yield_bags_ha" "lodging"      
#> [5] "yield_t_ha"   
#> 
#> $row.names
#> [1] 1 2 3 4
#> 
#> $class
#> [1] "data.frame"



3.8.2 A factor is an integer with labels

typeof(block)
#> [1] "integer"
attributes(block)
#> $levels
#> [1] "1" "2" "3"
#> 
#> $class
#> [1] "factor"
unclass(block)
#> [1] 1 2 3 1 2 3 1 2 3
#> attr(,"levels")
#> [1] "1" "2" "3"



3.8.3 A matrix is a vector with dimensions

v <- 1:6
dim(v) <- c(2, 3)
v
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    3    5
#> [2,]    2    4    6

Assigning the dim attribute to a vector turns it into a matrix. This pattern (complex structures as simple vectors plus attributes) explains much of R’s consistency.

text:
3.9 Exercises

Selecting from vectors. With the vector height_cm <- c(HB01 = 212, HB02 = 230, HB03 = 198, HB04 = 241, HB05 = 225), select: (a) the height of HB03; (b) all but HB01; (c) the hybrids taller than 220 cm; (d) the name of the tallest hybrid.







TipSolution






height_cm <- c(HB01 = 212, HB02 = 230, HB03 = 198, HB04 = 241, HB05 = 225)
height_cm["HB03"]
#> HB03 
#>  198
height_cm[-1]
#> HB02 HB03 HB04 HB05 
#>  230  198  241  225
height_cm[height_cm > 220]
#> HB02 HB04 HB05 
#>  230  241  225
names(which.max(height_cm))
#> [1] "HB04"

TipSolution






severity <- factor(
  c("low", "high", "medium", "low", "high", "high"),
  levels = c("low", "medium", "high"),
  ordered = TRUE
)
table(severity)
#> severity
#>    low medium   high 
#>      2      1      3
sum(severity > "low")
#> [1] 4

TipSolution






freq <- colMeans(markers) / 2
freq
#>  snp1  snp2  snp3  snp4  snp5 
#> 0.375 0.625 0.875 0.250 0.125
selected <- names(freq)[freq >= 0.2 & freq <= 0.8]
markers[, selected, drop = FALSE]
#>      snp1 snp2 snp4
#> HB01    0    1    1
#> HB02    1    1    0
#> HB03    2    1    0
#> HB04    0    2    1





Lists. From the trial list, extract: (a) the number of blocks multiplied by the number of locations; (b) the genotype of HB04 at snp2. Explain why trial["n_blocks"] * length(trial["locations"]) does not give the expected result.







TipSolution

#> [1] 8
trial$markers["HB04", "snp2"]
#> [1] 2

trial["n_blocks"] is a list, and lists do not support arithmetic (error). And length(trial["locations"]) is 1, the number of elements in the sublist, not 2, the number of locations.

title: 4  Packages and the ecosystem
text:
4.1 What a package is
A package is an organised bundle of functions, documentation, example data and tests, distributed in a standard format. Everything we have used so far (mean(), lm(), factor()) comes from packages that ship with R, such as base and stats. The community’s thousands of packages extend R into virtually any field, quantitative genetics included: lme4, sommer, AlphaSimR, BGLR and asreml itself.
Two concepts that are often confused:

Repository: the online “catalogue” packages are downloaded from. The main ones are CRAN (the official repository, with over 20,000 automatically checked packages), Bioconductor (specialised in bioinformatics and genomics) and GitHub (code under development, with no formal review). r-universe is a platform that builds packages straight from GitHub, widely used by projects such as rOpenSci.
Library: the folder on your computer where installed packages are stored.


.libPaths()   # where this R installation's libraries live
#> [1] "/home/ana/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/4.6"
#> [2] "/usr/lib/R/library"

There are usually two: a personal one (where the packages you install go) and a system one (with the packages that ship with R).

title: 4  Packages and the ecosystem
text:
4.2 Installing packages
Installing means downloading the package and storing it in the library. You do it once per computer (and again when you want to update):

# From CRAN
install.packages("janitor")
install.packages(c("readxl", "lubridate"))   # several at once

# From Bioconductor (needs the BiocManager package)
install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("SNPRelate")

# From GitHub ("user/repository" format)
install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("rstudio/gt")







NotePackage intent: pak



Problem it solves. Installing packages from different sources requires different tools (install.packages(), BiocManager, remotes), and dependency failures show up halfway through the installation, sometimes leaving the library half-updated.
Philosophy. pak offers a single function, pak::pak(), that understands packages from CRAN ("dplyr"), Bioconductor ("bioc::SNPRelate") and GitHub ("user/repo"). It resolves every dependency before installing, downloads in parallel and, on Linux, tells you which operating-system libraries are missing.
Why this one and not the alternatives. install.packages() remains perfectly valid for CRAN, and it is what you will see in most tutorials. pak wins when a project mixes sources or when installing a package with many dependencies fails in obscure ways. The remotes package, long used to install from GitHub, has in practice been superseded by pak.








WarningNever put install.packages() in an analysis script



Installing is an action on the computer, not part of the analysis. A script that reinstalls packages every time it runs is slow, may update versions without you noticing and fails without internet. Install from the console; record the versions with renv (see below).



4.2.1 ASReml-R is a special case
asreml is not on CRAN: it is commercial software from VSN International, distributed under licence. It is installed from the file VSN provides, and the licence must be activated once per machine. We will cover the details in lesson 44 and in the installation appendix.

text:
4.3 Loading packages
Loading makes the package’s functions available in the current session. You do it in every session in which you use the package:

library(janitor)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'janitor'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     chisq.test, fisher.test

Now janitor’s functions can be called by name:

clean_names(data.frame(`Produtividade (sc/ha)` = 62.4, check.names = FALSE))
#>   produtividade_sc_ha
#> 1                62.4

The alternative is not loading it and calling the function with the :: operator, as we already did with usethis::create_project():

janitor::make_clean_names(c("Planting Date", "Yield (kg/ha)", "Plant Height"))
#> [1] "planting_date" "yield_kg_ha"   "plant_height"








Form
When to use it




library(package) at the top of the script
packages used many times in the script (dplyr, ggplot2)


package::function()
functions used once or twice, or when the name could be ambiguous



require() also loads packages, but it only returns FALSE (with a warning) when the package is missing, instead of stopping with an error. In analysis scripts prefer library(): if a package is missing, it is better to find out on the first line.

4.3.1 Conflicts: two functions with the same name
When two loaded packages have functions with the same name, the one from the last loaded package wins, and R warns you that it “masks” the earlier one:

library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

The message says, for example, that dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter(). From now on, filter() means the dplyr version. If you need the other one, use :::

stats::filter(1:10, rep(1/3, 3))   # moving average, the time-series function

Conflicts like these cause confusing errors (“unused argument”, “object not found”) when you think you are calling one function and are calling another. The conflicted package turns any conflict into an explicit error, forcing you to choose:

library(conflicted)
conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter)



4.3.2 Which version do I have?

packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '1.2.1'
packageVersion("janitor")
#> [1] '2.2.1'

sessionInfo() shows the R version, the operating system and every loaded package. Copy its output whenever you ask for help or report a bug: it answers half the questions anyone would ask.

sessionInfo()

text:
4.4 The tidyverse






NotePackage intent: tidyverse



Problem it solves. Base R grew over decades, with functions written by different people with different conventions: argument order varies, names mix styles (read.csv, readRDS, nchar) and each function returns a different kind of object. That slows down learning and makes code hard to read.
Philosophy. The tidyverse is a collection of packages that share a grammar:

the data always come first, in a table (tibble), which lets functions be chained with the pipe;
each function does one thing, with a verb for a name (filter, select, mutate, summarise);
names use snake_case, and functions in the same family start the same way (str_detect, str_replace; read_csv, read_tsv);
code is written to be read by people, not just executed.

Why this one and not the alternatives. For trial data analysis, the tidyverse offers the gentlest learning curve and the largest community, with extensive documentation in Portuguese and English. Base R remains essential (and we will use it whenever it is simpler), and data.table is the choice for tables with tens of millions of rows. The lab adopts the tidyverse as its standard because the code stays readable for whoever reviews it, including yourself a year from now.


library(tidyverse) loads the core packages in one go:

library(tidyverse)
#> ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ─────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0.9000 ──
#> ✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
#> ✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
#> ✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
#> ✔ purrr     1.2.2     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
#> ── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
#> ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
#> ✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
#> ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

text:
4.5 The pipe |>
The pipe passes the result on its left as the first argument of the function on its right. Read |> as “and then”:

yield_bags_ha <- c(62.4, 58.1, 70.3, 66.0, 65.8, NA)

# Without the pipe: we read from the inside out
round(mean(yield_bags_ha * 60 / 1000, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 2)
#> [1] 3.87

# With the pipe: we read top to bottom, in the order things happen
(yield_bags_ha * 60 / 1000) |>
  mean(na.rm = TRUE) |>
  round(digits = 2)
#> [1] 3.87

Both forms do exactly the same thing. The pipe’s advantage grows with the number of steps: in an analysis with ten transformations, the nested version becomes unreadable, and creating ten intermediate objects clutters the environment.

4.5.1 |> or %>%?
You will find two pipes in R code:




|> (native)
%>% (magrittr)




Available since
R 4.1 (2021)
2014, via a package


Needs a package?
no
magrittr (loaded by the tidyverse)


Placeholder
_ (only in a named argument)
.




# When the data do not go in the first argument, use the named placeholder
cars |> lm(dist ~ speed, data = _) |> coef()
#> (Intercept)       speed 
#>  -17.579095    3.932409

The lab standard is |>. It does not depend on a package and is slightly faster. Set RStudio’s shortcut (Ctrl + Shift + M) to insert it: Tools > Global Options > Code and tick Use native pipe operator.






TipPipe style



Put each step on its own line, with |> at the end of the previous line and the next line indented by two spaces. Avoid chains of more than 8 to 10 steps; if it gets long, create an intermediate object with a name that explains what it is.

title: 4  Packages and the ecosystem
text:
4.6 Reproducible versions with renv
Imagine you finished your dissertation analysis in 2026. In 2028, a reviewer asks for a change. In the meantime you have updated R and every package, and one function changed its behaviour: the script no longer runs, or worse, it runs and gives a different result.






NotePackage intent: renv



Problem it solves. By default, every project on your computer uses the same library. Updating a package for a new project can break an old one, and there is no record of which versions each project used.
Philosophy. renv gives each project its own library and a renv.lock file that records the exact version of every package used. Whoever clones the project runs renv::restore() and gets the same versions. The workflow has three verbs: init (activate), snapshot (record the current state) and restore (recreate the recorded state).
Why this one and not the alternatives. Containers (Docker) freeze the whole operating system and are the most complete solution, but they demand infrastructure and know-how that most analyses do not need. renv solves the part that breaks most often, package versions, without leaving R. It replaced the older packrat.


The workflow, always inside the project:

renv::init()       # once: creates the project library and renv.lock

# ... you install packages and work as usual ...
install.packages("lme4")

renv::snapshot()   # records the versions in use in renv.lock
renv::status()     # shows whether renv.lock is in sync with what the code uses

# On another computer, after cloning the project:
renv::restore()    # installs exactly the versions in renv.lock

renv.lock is a text file and goes into Git. The renv/library/ folder, which holds the packages themselves, does not: it is recreated by restore().

4.7 How to evaluate an unfamiliar package
Found a package that promises to solve your problem? Before basing a thesis on it, ask five questions:

Where does it live? CRAN and Bioconductor require packages to pass automatic checks on several systems. A package that only lives on GitHub has passed none.
Is it alive? When was the last release? Do the GitHub issues get answers?
Who maintains it? An established research group, a company, a single person?
Does it have documentation and a paper? Serious scientific packages usually have a vignette and a published paper describing the methods (like those for lme4, sommer and BGLR, which are in this book’s references).
How many dependencies does it bring? Each dependency is one more thing that can break.


# How many packages does dplyr require, directly and indirectly?
deps <- tools::package_dependencies("dplyr", db = installed.packages(), recursive = TRUE)
length(deps$dplyr)
#> [1] 19

4.8 Under the hood

4.8.1 The search path
When you type a function name, R looks for it in a sequence of environments, the search path:

search()
#>  [1] ".GlobalEnv"        "package:lubridate" "package:forcats"  
#>  [4] "package:stringr"   "package:purrr"     "package:readr"    
#>  [7] "package:tidyr"     "package:tibble"    "package:ggplot2"  
#> [10] "package:tidyverse" "package:dplyr"     "package:janitor"  
#> [13] "package:stats"     "package:graphics"  "package:grDevices"
#> [16] "package:utils"     "package:datasets"  "package:methods"  
#> [19] "Autoloads"         "package:base"

The search starts in the global environment (.GlobalEnv, where your objects live) and goes through the packages in reverse order of loading. That is why the last loaded package “wins” a conflict.


4.8.2 :: loads without attaching
Using package::function() loads the package’s namespace (its code is available in memory), but does not put it on the search path:

"package:lubridate" %in% search()     # the tidyverse attached lubridate
#> [1] TRUE
"package:readxl" %in% search()        # readxl is not attached
#> [1] FALSE
invisible(readxl::excel_sheets(here::here("data", "raw", "milho_met_2024.xlsx")))
"readxl" %in% loadedNamespaces()      # but now it is loaded
#> [1] TRUE
"package:readxl" %in% search()        # and is still off the search path
#> [1] FALSE



4.8.3 Where each file of a package lives
system.file() finds files installed with a package, such as example data:

system.file("extdata", package = "readxl") |> list.files()
#>  [1] "clippy.xls"    "clippy.xlsx"   "datasets.xls"  "datasets.xlsx"
#>  [5] "deaths.xls"    "deaths.xlsx"   "geometry.xls"  "geometry.xlsx"
#>  [9] "type-me.xls"   "type-me.xlsx"

4.9 Exercises

Installing and loading. Explain, in one sentence each, why these snippets are wrong in an analysis script and how to fix them:


install.packages("dplyr")
library(dplyr)


require(lme4)
model <- lmer(yield ~ (1 | hybrid), data = trial)







TipSolution





In the first, install.packages() reinstalls the package every time the script runs; installing should be done once from the console and recorded with renv::snapshot(). Only library(dplyr) stays.
In the second, if lme4 is not installed, require() returns FALSE with a warning and the error only appears on the next line (could not find function "lmer"), far from its cause. With library(lme4) the error appears on the right line.




Pipe. Rewrite with the native pipe, one step per line:


round(sqrt(sum((c(2.1, 3.4, 2.8) - mean(c(2.1, 3.4, 2.8)))^2) / 2), 3)







TipSolution






x <- c(2.1, 3.4, 2.8)

((x - mean(x))^2) |>
  sum() |>
  (\(total) total / 2)() |>
  sqrt() |>
  round(digits = 3)
#> [1] 0.651

sd(x) |> round(3)   # and, of course, there is already a function for this
#> [1] 0.651

The step (\(total) total / 2)() is an anonymous function, which we will see in detail in lesson 14. The exercise shows a limit of the pipe: when a step is not a simple function call, the piped version can look stranger than the original. With well-named intermediate objects, the calculation is clearer.




Conflicts. After library(dplyr), which function does filter() call? And lag()? Use search() and environment(filter) to confirm.







TipSolution






environment(filter)
#> <environment: namespace:dplyr>
environment(lag)
#> <environment: namespace:dplyr>

Both come from dplyr, which was attached after stats and therefore appears before it in search().




Evaluation. Pick a genetics package you use or plan to use (for example sommer, AGHmatrix or rrBLUP). Answer the five questions from “How to evaluate an unfamiliar package” for it.







TipGuidance





Start with packageDescription("sommer") (version, maintainer, date) and citation("sommer") (reference paper). The package’s CRAN page shows the results of the automatic checks, and its GitHub repository shows recent activity.

citation("sommer")
#> To cite package 'sommer' in publications use:
#>

#>   using the R package sommer." _PLoS ONE_, *11*, 1-15.
#> 
#> A BibTeX entry for LaTeX users is
#> 
#>   @Article{,
#>     title = {Genome assisted prediction of quantitative traits using the R package sommer},
#>     author = {Covarrubias-Pazaran Giovanny},
#>     journal = {PLoS ONE},
#>     year = {2016},
#>     volume = {11},
#>     pages = {1-15},
