5.2 readr: reading text files






NotePackage intent: readr



Problem it solves. Base R’s reading functions (read.csv(), read.table()) are slow on large files, guess types in an opaque way, change column names without warning and, in older R versions, turned all text into factors.
Philosophy. readr reads the file, shows what it guessed about each column and returns a tibble. If a value does not fit the expected type, it neither stops nor hides it: it marks the value as NA and records what happened in problems(). Regional settings (decimal mark, encoding, date format) are gathered in a single object, locale().
Why this one and not the alternatives. read.csv() works and you will see it a lot, but it requires more care with types and names. data.table::fread() is even faster and will be covered in lesson 18, together with arrow for large files. For everyday trial data, readr strikes the best balance of speed, transparency and integration with the rest of the tidyverse.


Let us start with the simplest file:

locais <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "locais.csv"))
#> Rows: 4 Columns: 6
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr (3): local, municipio, uf
#> dbl (3): latitude, longitude, altitude_m
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
locais
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   local       municipio   uf    latitude longitude altitude_m
#>   <chr>       <chr>       <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 vicosa      Viçosa      MG       -20.8     -42.9        650
#> 2 sete_lagoas Sete Lagoas MG       -19.5     -44.2        730
#> 3 rio_verde   Rio Verde   GO       -17.8     -50.9        750
#> 4 londrina    Londrina    PR       -23.3     -51.2        585

The Column specification message shows what readr concluded: local, municipio and uf (state) are text (chr); latitude, longitude and altitude_m are numbers (dbl). That conclusion comes from reading the first 1000 rows.

5.2.1 Specifying the types
In production scripts it is better to state the types than to let them be guessed. That way, if the file changes, you find out at reading time rather than three steps later:

locais <- read_csv(
  here("data", "raw", "locais.csv"),
  col_types = cols(
    local = col_character(),
    municipio = col_character(),
    uf = col_factor(),
    altitude_m = col_integer(),
    .default = col_double()
  )
)
locais
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   local       municipio   uf    latitude longitude altitude_m
#>   <chr>       <chr>       <fct>    <dbl>     <dbl>      <int>
#> 1 vicosa      Viçosa      MG       -20.8     -42.9        650
#> 2 sete_lagoas Sete Lagoas MG       -19.5     -44.2        730
#> 3 rio_verde   Rio Verde   GO       -17.8     -50.9        750
#> 4 londrina    Londrina    PR       -23.3     -51.2        585

text:
5.3 The “Brazilian-style” CSV
Spreadsheets exported from computers set up in Portuguese (and many other languages) usually use a semicolon as separator (because the comma is already the decimal mark) and often the latin1 encoding (ISO-8859-1) instead of UTF-8. Let us see what happens when we read the soybean trial naively:

soy_wrong <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "soja_ensaio_2025.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
#> Warning: One or more parsing issues, call `problems()` on your data frame for details,
#> e.g.:
#>   dat <- vroom(...)
#>   problems(dat)
dim(soy_wrong)
#> [1] 120   1
names(soy_wrong)
#> [1] "Local;Cultivar;Bloco;Produtividade (sc/ha);Peso 100 sementes (g);Dias at\xe9 matura\xe7\xe3o;Acamamento;Data de semeadura"

A table with a single column, whose name is the whole header line. read_csv() looked for commas to split the columns, but the file uses ;. The accents also show up as \xe7, a sign of the wrong encoding.

5.3.1 Step one: separator and decimal mark
read_delim() accepts any separator, and locale() states the numeric convention:

soy <- read_delim(
  here("data", "raw", "soja_ensaio_2025.csv"),
  delim = ";",
  locale = locale(decimal_mark = ","),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
soy |> select(Bloco, `Produtividade (sc/ha)`, `Peso 100 sementes (g)`) |> head(3)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   Bloco `Produtividade (sc/ha)` `Peso 100 sementes (g)`
#>   <dbl>                   <dbl>                   <dbl>
#> 1     1                    56.1                    12.7
#> 2     2                    59.1                    15.8
#> 3     3                    55.5                    15.5
unique(soy$Local)
#> [1] "Vi\xe7osa" "Rio Verde"

The columns are split and the decimals are right (56.1, not 561), but “Viçosa” still shows up as "Vi\xe7osa". We used show_col_types = FALSE and printed only a few columns because, with the wrong encoding, R cannot even print the whole table: the accented names break printing with an invalid multibyte string error, another symptom of the same problem.


5.3.2 Step two: the encoding
An encoding is the table that translates bytes into letters. In UTF-8, “ç” takes two bytes; in latin1, one. Reading a latin1 file as if it were UTF-8 produces those odd characters. When you do not know the encoding, readr can estimate it:

guess_encoding(here("data", "raw", "soja_ensaio_2025.csv"))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   encoding   confidence
#>   <chr>           <dbl>
#> 1 ISO-8859-1        0.4

We state the encoding in the same locale():

soy <- read_delim(
  here("data", "raw", "soja_ensaio_2025.csv"),
  delim = ";",
  locale = locale(decimal_mark = ",", encoding = "latin1")
)
#> Rows: 120 Columns: 8
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ";"
#> chr (4): Local, Cultivar, Acamamento, Data de semeadura
#> dbl (4): Bloco, Produtividade (sc/ha), Peso 100 sementes (g), Dias até matur...
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
soy
#> # A tibble: 120 × 8
#>    Local  Cultivar  Bloco `Produtividade (sc/ha)` `Peso 100 sementes (g)`
#>    <chr>  <chr>     <dbl>                   <dbl>                   <dbl>
#>  1 Viçosa "sj-01"       1                    56.1                    12.7
#>  2 Viçosa "SJ-01"       2                    59.1                    15.8
#>  3 Viçosa "SJ 01"       3                    55.5                    15.5
#>  4 Viçosa "SJ-01"       4                    58.8                    16.2
#>  5 Viçosa "SJ-02"       1                    65.5                    16.5
#>  6 Viçosa " SJ-02 "     2                    51.7                    16.5
#>  7 Viçosa "SJ-02"       3                    60.6                    16.9
#>  8 Viçosa "SJ-02"       4                    61.8                    14.7
#>  9 Viçosa "SJ-03"       1                    57.1                    14.1
#> 10 Viçosa "SJ-03"       2                    56.7                    15.8
#> # ℹ 110 more rows
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: `Dias até maturação` <dbl>, Acamamento <chr>,
#> #   `Data de semeadura` <chr>
unique(soy$Local)
#> [1] "Viçosa"    "Rio Verde"

Now “Viçosa” is correct. Internally, readr converted everything to UTF-8, the standard for modern R.






TipShortcut: read_csv2()



read_csv2() already assumes ; as separator and a decimal comma. For this file, read_csv2(file, locale = locale(encoding = "latin1")) would give the same result. We prefer read_delim() in the text because it makes every decision explicit.




5.3.3 When reading fails: problems()
The Data de semeadura (sowing date) column was read as text. Let us ask for it to be read as a date in the Brazilian format (day/month/year):

soy_dates <- read_delim(
  here("data", "raw", "soja_ensaio_2025.csv"),
  delim = ";",
  locale = locale(decimal_mark = ",", encoding = "latin1"),
  col_types = cols(`Data de semeadura` = col_date(format = "%d/%m/%Y"))
)
#> Warning: One or more parsing issues, call `problems()` on your data frame for details,
#> e.g.:
#>   dat <- vroom(...)
#>   problems(dat)

The warning says there were problems. Instead of ignoring it, investigate:

problems(soy_dates) |> select(-file)
#> # A tibble: 23 × 4
#>      row   col expected           actual    
#>    <int> <int> <chr>              <chr>     
#>  1     2     8 date like %d/%m/%Y 2024-10-16
#>  2     8     8 date like %d/%m/%Y 2024-10-15
#>  3    10     8 date like %d/%m/%Y 2024-10-17
#>  4    12     8 date like %d/%m/%Y 2024-10-15
#>  5    30     8 date like %d/%m/%Y 2024-10-16
#>  6    32     8 date like %d/%m/%Y 2024-10-15
#>  7    34     8 date like %d/%m/%Y 2024-10-16
#>  8    43     8 date like %d/%m/%Y 2024-10-15
#>  9    44     8 date like %d/%m/%Y 2024-10-16
#> 10    46     8 date like %d/%m/%Y 2024-10-15
#> # ℹ 13 more rows

Some dates were typed in the international format (2024-10-16) and do not fit %d/%m/%Y. readr turned them into NA. Had you not looked at problems(), you would have lost those dates without noticing. In lesson 8 we will see how to read dates in mixed formats with lubridate; for now, the lesson is: every reading warning deserves a look at problems().


5.3.4 Coded missing values
By default, readr treats empty cells and the text "NA" as missing. If the spreadsheet uses other codes, list them in the na argument:

read_csv(file, na = c("", "NA", "-", "n/a", "lost"))

5.4 readxl: Excel spreadsheets






NotePackage intent: readxl



Problem it solves. Much field data arrives as .xlsx, often with several sheets, decorative headers and merged cells. Converting each sheet to CSV by hand is slow and leaves no record.
Philosophy. readxl reads .xls and .xlsx without depending on Excel or Java, following readr’s logic: it guesses types, accepts na and col_types and returns a tibble. It only reads, never writes, and does that well.
Why this one and not the alternatives. openxlsx and writexl also read or write Excel; openxlsx is great when you need to create formatted spreadsheets, and we used it to generate this course’s data. For reading, readxl is the simplest and most robust, and it is installed with the tidyverse. Old Java-based packages (xlsx, XLConnect) cause installation problems and should be avoided.



library(readxl)

maize_file <- here("data", "raw", "milho_met_2024.xlsx")
excel_sheets(maize_file)
#> [1] "Londrina"    "Rio Verde"   "Sete Lagoas" "Viçosa"

The file has one sheet per location. Let us read the first one with no options:

read_excel(maize_file, sheet = "Viçosa")

#>  2 <NA>                                      <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA> 
#>  3 Híbrido                                   Bloco Prod… Altu… Flor… Data… Obs  
#>  4 HB01                                      1     9404  236   63    13/1… <NA>

#>  7 HB02                                      1     8104  239   61    13/1… <NA>

The first row of the sheet became the name of the first column and the others got names ...2, ...3. Opening the file in Excel, we see two note rows and a blank row before the header. The skip argument skips those rows:

maize_vicosa <- read_excel(maize_file, sheet = "Viçosa", skip = 3)
maize_vicosa
#> # A tibble: 60 × 7
#>    Híbrido Bloco `Prod (kg/ha)` `Altura (cm)` `Florescimento (dias)`

Now look at the Londrina sheet:

maize_londrina <- read_excel(maize_file, sheet = "Londrina", skip = 3)
maize_londrina
#> # A tibble: 60 × 7
#>    Híbrido Bloco `Prod (kg/ha)` `Altura (cm)` `Florescimento (dias)`

maize_londrina |>
  filter(is.na(as.numeric(`Prod (kg/ha)`))) |>
  select(Híbrido, Bloco, `Prod (kg/ha)`, Obs)
#> Warning: There was 1 warning in `filter()`.
#> ℹ In argument: `is.na(as.numeric(`Prod (kg/ha)`))`.

maize_londrina <- read_excel(
  maize_file,
  sheet = "Londrina",
  skip = 3,
  na = c("", "-", "perdida")
)
maize_londrina

read_excel(file, sheet = 2)                  # sheet by position
read_excel(file, range = "B4:F64")           # just a rectangle of cells
read_excel(file, range = cell_cols("A:D"))   # just some columns
read_excel(file, col_types = c("text", "numeric", "numeric", "skip"))

maize_2024 <- excel_sheets(maize_file) |>
  set_names() |>
  map(\(sheet) read_excel(maize_file, sheet = sheet, skip = 3, na = c("", "-", "perdida"))) |>

5.5 janitor: clean column names
Names like `Prod (kg/ha)` and `Data Plantio` need backticks in code, are easy to mistype and break the lab style.






NotePackage intent: janitor



Problem it solves. Data coming from spreadsheets have column names with spaces, accents, parentheses, capitals and duplicates, as well as empty rows and columns and totals mixed in with the data.
Philosophy. janitor gathers small “cleaning” functions that each do one thing and fit into the pipe. The most used one, clean_names(), converts every name to snake_case, strips accents and symbols and resolves repeated names.
Why this one and not the alternatives. Renaming column by column with dplyr::rename() works, but it is laborious and must be redone whenever the spreadsheet changes. clean_names() applies a consistent rule to any spreadsheet, in one line. janitor also offers remove_empty(), get_dupes() and tabyl(), which we will use throughout the course.



library(janitor)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'janitor'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     chisq.test, fisher.test

maize_2024 <- clean_names(maize_2024)
names(maize_2024)
#> [1] "local"              "hibrido"            "bloco"             
#> [4] "prod_kg_ha"         "altura_cm"          "florescimento_dias"
#> [7] "data_plantio"       "obs"

soy <- clean_names(soy)
names(soy)
#> [1] "local"               "cultivar"            "bloco"              
#> [4] "produtividade_sc_ha" "peso_100_sementes_g" "dias_ate_maturacao" 
#> [7] "acamamento"          "data_de_semeadura"

Híbrido became hibrido (hybrid), Prod (kg/ha) became prod_kg_ha and Dias até maturação (days to maturity) became dias_ate_maturacao. Every following lesson uses names in this format.
Two other cleaning functions worth knowing:

# Rows duplicated on the combination of columns that should be unique
get_dupes(maize_2024, local, hibrido, bloco)
#> No duplicate combinations found of: local, hibrido, bloco
#> # A tibble: 0 × 9
#> # ℹ 9 variables: local <chr>, hibrido <chr>, bloco <dbl>, dupe_count <int>,
#> #   prod_kg_ha <dbl>, altura_cm <dbl>, florescimento_dias <dbl>,
#> #   data_plantio <chr>, obs <chr>

# Drop entirely empty rows and columns
remove_empty(maize_2024, which = c("rows", "cols")) |> dim()
#> [1] 240   8

No duplicates: each combination of location, hybrid and block appears once, as expected in a block design.

5.6.1 SPSS, Stata and SAS: haven
Data from collaborators in other fields sometimes arrive in the formats of commercial statistics software. The haven package reads and writes those files and preserves value labels, which are common in those programs:

library(haven)

# Create an example .sav file in a temporary folder
sav_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".sav")

  reaction = labelled(c(1, 3, 2), c(resistant = 1, moderate = 2, susceptible = 3))
) |>
  write_sav(sav_file)

spss_data <- read_sav(sav_file)
spss_data

#> 3 SJ-03    2 [moderate]

5.7 Saving results
After reading and cleaning, you will want to save the result. The format depends on who will use the file:








Format
Function
When to use it




CSV
write_csv()
exchanging data with any software; works well in Git


Semicolon CSV
write_csv2()
sending to someone who will open it in a locale with a decimal comma


RDS
write_rds()
keeping an R object exactly as it is (types, factors, lists)


Excel
writexl::write_xlsx()
handing spreadsheets to collaborators




tmp_dir <- tempdir()

write_csv(maize_2024, file.path(tmp_dir, "maize_2024.csv"))
write_rds(maize_2024, file.path(tmp_dir, "maize_2024.rds"))
writexl::write_xlsx(maize_2024, file.path(tmp_dir, "maize_2024.xlsx"))

# RDS preserves the tibble and the types; the CSV must be read and interpreted again
identical(read_rds(file.path(tmp_dir, "maize_2024.rds")), maize_2024)
#> [1] TRUE

The lab rule: intermediate files between scripts of the same project go in RDS (fast, keeps types); output files that other people will open go in CSV or Excel.

5.8 A checklist after every import
Every read of new data should end with a quick inspection. glimpse() shows each column horizontally, with its type and first values:

glimpse(maize_2024)
#> Rows: 240

5.9 Under the hood

5.9.1 How readr guesses types
readr examines the first 1000 rows of each column and picks the most restrictive type that fits every value, in the order logical, integer, double, date, text. If the first “odd” value is on row 5000, the column will be typed wrongly. The guess_max argument enlarges the sample:

read_csv(file, guess_max = Inf)   # examines every row (slower)

The specification used is stored in the object and can be reused:

spec(locais)
#> cols(
#>   .default = col_double(),
#>   local = col_character(),
#>   municipio = col_character(),
#>   uf = col_factor(levels = NULL, ordered = FALSE, include_na = FALSE),
#>   latitude = col_double(),
#>   longitude = col_double(),
#>   altitude_m = col_integer()
#> )



5.9.2 read.csv() makes different choices

locais_base <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "locais.csv"))

Diagnosis. Why does the read below produce a text Prod (kg/ha) column, and why is that dangerous if you compute the mean right after with as.numeric()?


read_excel(maize_file, sheet = "Londrina", skip = 3)







TipSolution





The codes "-" and "perdida" make the whole column be read as text. If you apply as.numeric() afterwards, they become NA with a generic warning, and the information about why the value is missing is lost. Worse: if there were a number typed with a decimal comma ("9.512,3"), it would also become NA and go unnoticed among the expected codes. Declaring the codes in na = c("-", "perdida") and keeping the Obs column preserves the information and makes any other unexpected text still show up as a problem.

text:
6.2 The dplyr grammar






NotePackage intent: dplyr



Problem it solves. Manipulating tables in base R means combining [, $, subset(), aggregate(), tapply() and order(), each with its own logic. The resulting code is hard to read and to change.
Philosophy. dplyr offers a small set of verbs, each with a single responsibility, that take a table as their first argument and return a table. Inside the verbs, columns are referred to by name, without quotes and without $. Combined with the pipe, the verbs form sentences that read like a description of the analysis: “take the trial, keep Londrina, group by hybrid, summarise yield”.
Why this one and not the alternatives. Base R can do everything, but with more reading effort. data.table is faster and more concise, at the cost of a denser syntax; we will meet it in lesson 18. dplyr also works as an interface to databases and to duckdb, so the same code serves tables that do not fit in memory.


The verbs we will see today:



Verb
Acts on
What it does




filter()
rows
keeps rows that meet conditions


select()
columns
picks, drops or renames columns


mutate()
columns
creates or modifies columns


arrange()
rows
sorts rows


summarise()
groups
reduces each group to one summary row



They all follow the same rules: the first argument is the table, the following ones describe what to do using column names, and the result is always a new table. The original table is never modified; to keep the result, assign it to an object.

maize |> relocate(prod_kg_ha, .after = hibrido) |> head(3)

6.5.1 Classifications: if_else() and case_when()
For two categories, if_else(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false):

maize |>
  mutate(lost = if_else(is.na(prod_kg_ha), "yes", "no")) |>
  count(lost)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   lost      n
#>   <chr> <int>
#> 1 no      233
#> 2 yes       7

For several ranges, case_when() evaluates the conditions in order and uses the first true one:

maize <- maize |>
  mutate(
    cycle = case_when(
      florescimento_dias <= 60 ~ "early",
      florescimento_dias <= 64 ~ "medium",
      florescimento_dias > 64  ~ "late",
      .default = NA_character_
    )
  )

count(maize, cycle)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   cycle      n
#>   <chr>  <int>
#> 1 early     56
#> 2 late      77
#> 3 medium   107

Because the conditions are evaluated in order, the second one (<= 64) only reaches those that did not match the first, that is, 61 to 64 days. .default sets the value when no condition is true.
Notice that this time we stored the result in maize: the cycle column will be available for the rest of the lesson.

6.7 summarise(): summarising

maize |>
  summarise(
    n_plots = n(),
    n_lost = sum(is.na(prod_kg_ha)),
    mean_kg_ha = mean(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_kg_ha = sd(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE),
    cv_pct = 100 * sd_kg_ha / mean_kg_ha
  )
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   n_plots n_lost mean_kg_ha sd_kg_ha cv_pct
#>     <int>  <int>      <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1     240      7      9464.    1109.   11.7

text:
6.8 Grouped operations
The .by argument makes any verb operate separately in each group:

maize |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_kg_ha = mean(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE),
    cv_pct = 100 * sd(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE) / mean_kg_ha,
    .by = local
  )
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   local           n mean_kg_ha cv_pct
#>   <chr>       <int>      <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Londrina       60      9194.  11.7 
#> 2 Rio Verde      60     10295.  10.1 
#> 3 Sete Lagoas    60      9532.   9.33
#> 4 Viçosa         60      8816.   9.74

Rio Verde was the highest-yielding environment and Viçosa the lowest. With two grouping variables we get the mean of each hybrid at each location:

means_hl <- maize |>
  summarise(
    mean_kg_ha = mean(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_blocks = sum(!is.na(prod_kg_ha)),
    .by = c(local, hibrido)
  )

means_hl
#> # A tibble: 80 × 4
#>    local    hibrido mean_kg_ha n_blocks
#>    <chr>    <chr>        <dbl>    <int>
#>  1 Londrina HB01         9508         3
#>  2 Londrina HB02         8776         3
#>  3 Londrina HB03         9842.        2
#>  4 Londrina HB04         8811.        3
#>  5 Londrina HB05         9300.        3
#>  6 Londrina HB06         8342         2
#>  7 Londrina HB07         9649.        3
#>  8 Londrina HB08         8961.        3
#>  9 Londrina HB09         9785.        3
#> 10 Londrina HB10        10606         3
#> # ℹ 70 more rows


6.8.1 group_by(): the traditional form
You will see a lot of code with group_by() followed by summarise(). The result is the same:

maize |>
  group_by(local) |>
  summarise(mean_kg_ha = mean(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   local       mean_kg_ha
#>   <chr>            <dbl>
#> 1 Londrina         9194.
#> 2 Rio Verde       10295.
#> 3 Sete Lagoas      9532.
#> 4 Viçosa           8816.

The difference is that group_by() creates a grouped table, which stays grouped in the following steps until you call ungroup(). That is useful in long chains, but a source of bugs when you forget the active grouping. The lab standard is .by for one-off operations and group_by() only when several consecutive steps use the same grouping.


6.8.2 Grouped mutate(): relative performance
In multi-environment trials, comparing raw yields across locations mixes the hybrid effect with the environment effect. A first step is to express each plot relative to the mean of its own location:

maize |>
  mutate(
    location_mean = mean(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE),
    deviation = prod_kg_ha - location_mean,
    relative_pct = 100 * prod_kg_ha / location_mean,
    .by = local
  ) |>
  select(local, hibrido, bloco, prod_kg_ha, location_mean, relative_pct) |>
  arrange(desc(relative_pct))
#> # A tibble: 240 × 6
#>    local       hibrido bloco prod_kg_ha location_mean relative_pct
#>    <chr>       <chr>   <dbl>      <dbl>         <dbl>        <dbl>
#>  1 Viçosa      HB16        3      11346         8816.         129.
#>  2 Londrina    HB10        2      11319         9194.         123.
#>  3 Londrina    HB16        1      11262         9194.         122.
#>  4 Londrina    HB10        3      11066         9194.         120.
#>  5 Rio Verde   HB18        2      12262        10295.         119.
#>  6 Rio Verde   HB20        3      12203        10295.         119.
#>  7 Sete Lagoas HB16        1      11299         9532.         119.
#>  8 Londrina    HB16        2      10886         9194.         118.
#>  9 Rio Verde   HB17        1      12115        10295.         118.
#> 10 Londrina    HB17        3      10770         9194.         117.
#> # ℹ 230 more rows

With .by, mean() inside mutate() is computed for each location, but the result goes back to every row of that location. That is the essential difference between summarise() (one row per group) and grouped mutate() (same number of rows, values computed per group).

6.10 Case study: ranking the hybrids
Question: which hybrids had the best average performance across the four locations, and were they consistent, or did they shine in a single environment?

ranking <- maize |>
  # 1. mean of each hybrid at each location
  summarise(mean_kg_ha = mean(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(local, hibrido)) |>
  # 2. rank of each hybrid within each location (1 = best)
  mutate(rank = min_rank(desc(mean_kg_ha)), .by = local) |>
  # 3. summary per hybrid across the four locations
  summarise(
    overall_mean_kg_ha = mean(mean_kg_ha),
    best_rank = min(rank),
    worst_rank = max(rank),
    times_in_top5 = sum(rank <= 5),
    .by = hibrido
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(overall_mean_kg_ha))

ranking

text:
6.11 Under the hood

6.11.1 Why dplyr understands unquoted names
In filter(maize, prod_kg_ha > 9000), prod_kg_ha is not an object in the global environment:

prod_kg_ha
#> Error:
#> ! object 'prod_kg_ha' not found

dplyr looks names up first among the table’s columns and only then in the environment. This mechanism, called data masking, is what makes the code so readable. It has one consequence: if a column and an object share a name, the column wins. To use the object, mark it with .env$:

threshold <- 10000
maize |> filter(prod_kg_ha > threshold) |> nrow()
#> [1] 69

prod_kg_ha <- 0   # an object with the same name as a column
maize |> filter(prod_kg_ha > .env$prod_kg_ha) |> nrow()   # compares with the object (0): all non-lost plots
#> [1] 233
rm(prod_kg_ha)

In lesson 16 we will see how to write functions that use dplyr, where this mechanism needs some extra care.


6.11.2 What a grouped table is

grouped <- group_by(maize, local)
class(grouped)
#> [1] "grouped_df" "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
group_vars(grouped)
#> [1] "local"
n_groups(grouped)
#> [1] 4

A grouped_df is a tibble with an extra attribute recording which rows belong to each group. The printout shows # Groups: local [4]; keep an eye on that line.


6.11.3 The base R equivalent

# dplyr
maize |> filter(local == "Londrina") |> summarise(m = mean(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>       m
#>   <dbl>
#> 1 9194.

# base R
mean(maize$prod_kg_ha[maize$local == "Londrina"], na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 9193.691
tapply(maize$prod_kg_ha, maize$local, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
#>    Londrina   Rio Verde Sete Lagoas      Viçosa 
#>    9193.691   10294.650    9532.224    8815.800

For a single calculation, base R is perfectly adequate. dplyr’s advantage shows when the steps pile up.

6.12 Exercises

Filters. How many Sete Lagoas plots yielded more than 10,000 kg/ha with plant height below 220 cm? And how many plots in the whole trial were lost?







TipSolution






maize |>
  filter(local == "Sete Lagoas", prod_kg_ha > 10000, altura_cm < 220) |>
  nrow()
#> [1] 9

maize |>
  filter(is.na(prod_kg_ha)) |>
  nrow()

New variable. Create the column stature with the values "short" (height under 210 cm), "medium" (210 to 230 cm) and "tall" (above 230 cm) and count how many plots fall in each combination of location and stature.







TipSolution






maize |>
  mutate(
    stature = case_when(
      altura_cm < 210 ~ "short",
      altura_cm <= 230 ~ "medium",
      .default = "tall"
    )
  ) |>
  count(local, stature)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 3
#>    local       stature     n
#>    <chr>       <chr>   <int>
#>  1 Londrina    medium     35
#>  2 Londrina    short      12

#>  9 Sete Lagoas tall       11

#> 11 Viçosa      short      10
#> 12 Viçosa      tall       15





Summary by hybrid. For each hybrid, compute the mean yield, the standard deviation and the number of non-lost plots, using all locations. Show the five hybrids with the highest mean.







TipSolution






maize |>
  summarise(
    mean = mean(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(prod_kg_ha)),
    .by = hibrido
  ) |>
  slice_max(mean, n = 5)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   hibrido   mean    sd     n
#>   <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> <int>
#> 1 HB16    10760.  628.    12
#> 2 HB17    10334. 1099.    11
#> 3 HB10    10054.  884.    11
#> 4 HB18     9991. 1103.    12
#> 5 HB20     9903.  969.    11





Relative performance. For each location, identify the hybrid with the highest yield relative to the location mean (using block means). Does any hybrid come out best at more than one location?







TipSolution






maize |>
  summarise(mean = mean(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(local, hibrido)) |>
  mutate(relative_pct = 100 * mean / mean(mean), .by = local) |>
  slice_max(relative_pct, n = 1, by = local)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   local       hibrido   mean relative_pct
#>   <chr>       <chr>    <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 Londrina    HB16    10963.         119.
#> 2 Rio Verde   HB17    11671          113.
#> 3 Sete Lagoas HB16    10782.         113.
#> 4 Viçosa      HB16    10357.         117.





Reading code. Describe in plain words, step by step, what the code below does and which question it answers.


maize |>
  filter(!is.na(prod_kg_ha)) |>
  mutate(yield_t_ha = prod_kg_ha / 1000) |>
  summarise(range = max(yield_t_ha) - min(yield_t_ha), .by = c(local, hibrido)) |>
  arrange(desc(range)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)







TipSolution





It removes the lost plots, converts yield to t/ha, computes for each hybrid at each location the difference between its best and worst block, sorts from the largest to the smallest difference and shows the first five. The question is: in which hybrid-location combinations were the blocks most discrepant? Very large values point to field heterogeneity or typing errors, and deserve to be checked before any analysis.

text:
Summary

dplyr verbs take a table, use unquoted column names and return a new table.
filter() picks rows and drops NA in conditions; select() picks columns with helpers such as starts_with() and where().
mutate() creates columns; case_when() classifies into ranges, evaluating conditions in order.
arrange() sorts; summarise() reduces to a summary.
.by applies any verb by group: summarise() returns one row per group, mutate() keeps every row.

7.1 What tidy data is
The same data can be organised in many ways. Here are three versions of the mean yield (t/ha) of two hybrids at two locations:

# Version A: one column per location
tribble(
  ~hybrid, ~vicosa, ~londrina,
  "HB01",  8.9,     9.5,
  "HB02",  8.2,     8.8
)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   hybrid vicosa londrina
#>   <chr>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 HB01      8.9      9.5
#> 2 HB02      8.2      8.8

# Version B: one row per hybrid and location
tribble(
  ~hybrid, ~location,  ~yield_t_ha,
  "HB01",  "vicosa",   8.9,
  "HB01",  "londrina", 9.5,
  "HB02",  "vicosa",   8.2,
  "HB02",  "londrina", 8.8
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   hybrid location yield_t_ha
#>   <chr>  <chr>         <dbl>
#> 1 HB01   vicosa          8.9
#> 2 HB01   londrina        9.5
#> 3 HB02   vicosa          8.2
#> 4 HB02   londrina        8.8

# Version C: hybrid and location glued into one column
tribble(
  ~plot,            ~yield_t_ha,
  "HB01_vicosa",    8.9,
  "HB01_londrina",  9.5,
  "HB02_vicosa",    8.2,
  "HB02_londrina",  8.8
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   plot          yield_t_ha
#>   <chr>              <dbl>
#> 1 HB01_vicosa          8.9
#> 2 HB01_londrina        9.5
#> 3 HB02_vicosa          8.2
#> 4 HB02_londrina        8.8

All three hold exactly the same information, but only version B is tidy. A table is tidy when it follows three rules:

Each variable is a column. In version A, “location” is a variable, but it is spread across the column names. In version C, two variables (hybrid and location) share the same column.
Each observation is a row. Here, the unit of observation is “one hybrid at one location”.
Each value is a cell.

Why does this matter? Because every tidyverse tool expects this format. With version B, filtering a location, computing the mean per hybrid, fitting lm(yield_t_ha ~ hybrid + location) or drawing a plot with one colour per location are direct operations. With version A, each one needs a different workaround.






TipWhat counts as “a variable” depends on the question



In a trial with yield, height and flowering, each trait is usually a column (an observation is a plot). But if the question is “what is the coefficient of variation of each trait at each location?”, it is more convenient to have a trait column and a value column. Moving from one format to the other is the core skill of this lesson.








NotePackage intent: tidyr



Problem it solves. Spreadsheets are laid out for human reading or for typing in the field, hardly ever for analysis: columns per year, per location or per replicate, compound identifiers, merged cells and missing combinations.
Philosophy. tidyr has a single goal: change the shape of a table without changing its information. Its functions come in small, symmetric families: pivot_longer/pivot_wider (lengthen and widen), separate_wider_*/unite (split and join columns), complete/drop_na/fill/replace_na (deal with missing values) and nest/unnest (tables inside tables).
Why this one and not the alternatives. Base R’s old reshape() and reshape2’s melt()/cast() solve the same problem with less clear interfaces; tidyr itself replaced its gather() and spread() with the easier-to-remember pivot_*(). You will still see gather()/spread() in older code; they work, but do not use them in new code.

7.2 pivot_longer(): from wide to long
The file for the 2024/25 season came with one yield column per location:

maize_2025_wide <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "milho_met_2025_largo.csv"))
#> Rows: 60 Columns: 6
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr (1): hibrido
#> dbl (5): bloco, prod_vicosa, prod_sete_lagoas, prod_rio_verde, prod_londrina
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
maize_2025_wide
#> # A tibble: 60 × 6
#>    hibrido bloco prod_vicosa prod_sete_lagoas prod_rio_verde prod_londrina
#>    <chr>   <dbl>       <dbl>            <dbl>          <dbl>         <dbl>
#>  1 HB01        1       10529            10057          10094          9622
#>  2 HB01        2        9540             9816          10677          7494
#>  3 HB01        3        9064             9795          10294          8074
#>  4 HB02        1        8489             8856           9874          8939
#>  5 HB02        2        8387             8348           9114          8938
#>  6 HB02        3        7595            10145           8733          8033
#>  7 HB03        1        8944             9941          10068          8176
#>  8 HB03        2        8288            10698          10291          8565
#>  9 HB03        3        8252             9720           8852         10030
#> 10 HB04        1        8084             9413           9572          7109
#> # ℹ 50 more rows

It is in version A’s format. To lengthen it, pivot_longer() needs three pieces of information:

cols: which columns will be “melted”;
names_to: the name of the new column that receives those columns’ names;
values_to: the name of the new column that receives their values.


maize_2025 <- maize_2025_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("prod_"),
    names_to = "local",
    values_to = "prod_kg_ha"
  )

maize_2025
#> # A tibble: 240 × 4
#>    hibrido bloco local            prod_kg_ha
#>    <chr>   <dbl> <chr>                 <dbl>
#>  1 HB01        1 prod_vicosa           10529
#>  2 HB01        1 prod_sete_lagoas      10057
#>  3 HB01        1 prod_rio_verde        10094
#>  4 HB01        1 prod_londrina          9622
#>  5 HB01        2 prod_vicosa            9540
#>  6 HB01        2 prod_sete_lagoas       9816
#>  7 HB01        2 prod_rio_verde        10677
#>  8 HB01        2 prod_londrina          7494
#>  9 HB01        3 prod_vicosa            9064
#> 10 HB01        3 prod_sete_lagoas       9795
#> # ℹ 230 more rows

We went from 60 rows and 6 columns to 240 rows and 4 columns. The local (location) column kept the prod_ prefix; the names_prefix argument removes it:

maize_2025 <- maize_2025_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("prod_"),
    names_to = "local",
    names_prefix = "prod_",
    values_to = "prod_kg_ha"
  )

count(maize_2025, local)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   local           n
#>   <chr>       <int>
#> 1 londrina       60
#> 2 rio_verde      60
#> 3 sete_lagoas    60
#> 4 vicosa         60

We keep the Portuguese column names local, hibrido and prod_kg_ha so that both seasons share the same structure.

7.2.1 Joining the two seasons
Both seasons now have the same structure, but the locations are written differently: "Viçosa" in the 2024 spreadsheet (the sheet name) and "vicosa" in the 2025 file (a code). The locais.csv file holds the mapping between the code and the municipality name:

locations <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "locais.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
locations |> select(local, municipio)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   local       municipio  
#>   <chr>       <chr>      
#> 1 vicosa      Viçosa     
#> 2 sete_lagoas Sete Lagoas
#> 3 rio_verde   Rio Verde  
#> 4 londrina    Londrina

We use this table to replace the code with the name. The left_join() function is the topic of lesson 10; for now, it is enough to know that it brings the columns of locations into the rows of maize_2025 with the same local:

maize_2025 <- maize_2025 |>
  left_join(select(locations, local, municipio), by = "local") |>
  mutate(local = municipio, safra = "2024/25", .keep = "unused")

maize_2025
#> # A tibble: 240 × 5
#>    hibrido bloco local       prod_kg_ha safra  
#>    <chr>   <dbl> <chr>            <dbl> <chr>  
#>  1 HB01        1 Viçosa           10529 2024/25
#>  2 HB01        1 Sete Lagoas      10057 2024/25
#>  3 HB01        1 Rio Verde        10094 2024/25
#>  4 HB01        1 Londrina          9622 2024/25
#>  5 HB01        2 Viçosa            9540 2024/25
#>  6 HB01        2 Sete Lagoas       9816 2024/25
#>  7 HB01        2 Rio Verde        10677 2024/25
#>  8 HB01        2 Londrina          7494 2024/25
#>  9 HB01        3 Viçosa            9064 2024/25
#> 10 HB01        3 Sete Lagoas       9795 2024/25
#> # ℹ 230 more rows

And we read the 2023/24 season as in lesson 5 (safra means season):

maize_file <- here("data", "raw", "milho_met_2024.xlsx")

maize_2024 <- excel_sheets(maize_file) |>
  set_names() |>
  map(\(sheet) read_excel(maize_file, sheet = sheet, skip = 3, na = c("", "-", "perdida"))) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "local") |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(safra = "2023/24")

bind_rows() stacks the two tables, matching columns by name. Columns that only exist in 2024 (height, flowering) get NA in the 2025 rows:

maize <- bind_rows(maize_2024, maize_2025)

maize |> count(safra, local)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   safra   local           n
#>   <chr>   <chr>       <int>
#> 1 2023/24 Londrina       60
#> 2 2023/24 Rio Verde      60
#> 3 2023/24 Sete Lagoas    60
#> 4 2023/24 Viçosa         60
#> 5 2024/25 Londrina       60
#> 6 2024/25 Rio Verde      60
#> 7 2024/25 Sete Lagoas    60
#> 8 2024/25 Viçosa         60

Now a single tidy table answers questions that would previously have required opening two files:

maize |>
  summarise(mean_kg_ha = mean(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(local, safra)) |>
  arrange(local, safra)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   local       safra   mean_kg_ha
#>   <chr>       <chr>        <dbl>
#> 1 Londrina    2023/24      9194.
#> 2 Londrina    2024/25      8589.
#> 3 Rio Verde   2023/24     10295.
#> 4 Rio Verde   2024/25      9981.
#> 5 Sete Lagoas 2023/24      9532.
#> 6 Sete Lagoas 2024/25      9119.
#> 7 Viçosa      2023/24      8816.
#> 8 Viçosa      2024/25      8366.



7.2.2 Several traits at once
In 2023/24 we measured three traits. To compute the same summary for all of them, we lengthen the table with a trait column:

maize_2024_long <- maize_2024 |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(prod_kg_ha, altura_cm, florescimento_dias),
    names_to = "trait",
    values_to = "value"
  )

maize_2024_long |>
  select(local, hibrido, bloco, trait, value)
#> # A tibble: 720 × 5
#>    local    hibrido bloco trait              value
#>    <chr>    <chr>   <dbl> <chr>              <dbl>
#>  1 Londrina HB01        1 prod_kg_ha          9779
#>  2 Londrina HB01        1 altura_cm            247
#>  3 Londrina HB01        1 florescimento_dias    64
#>  4 Londrina HB01        2 prod_kg_ha          9706
#>  5 Londrina HB01        2 altura_cm            210
#>  6 Londrina HB01        2 florescimento_dias    65
#>  7 Londrina HB01        3 prod_kg_ha          9039
#>  8 Londrina HB01        3 altura_cm            215
#>  9 Londrina HB01        3 florescimento_dias    66
#> 10 Londrina HB02        1 prod_kg_ha          8403
#> # ℹ 710 more rows

And a single summarise() produces the statistics for every trait at every location:

maize_2024_long |>
  summarise(
    mean = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    cv_pct = 100 * sd(value, na.rm = TRUE) / mean,
    .by = c(trait, local)
  ) |>
  arrange(trait, local)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 4
#>    trait              local          mean cv_pct
#>    <chr>              <chr>         <dbl>  <dbl>
#>  1 altura_cm          Londrina      221.    6.28
#>  2 altura_cm          Rio Verde     217.    5.75
#>  3 altura_cm          Sete Lagoas   222.    5.43
#>  4 altura_cm          Viçosa        222.    5.75
#>  5 florescimento_dias Londrina       65.8   4.02
#>  6 florescimento_dias Rio Verde      62.0   4.86
#>  7 florescimento_dias Sete Lagoas    61.8   5.68
#>  8 florescimento_dias Viçosa         61.9   4.56
#>  9 prod_kg_ha         Londrina     9194.   11.7 
#> 10 prod_kg_ha         Rio Verde   10295.   10.1 
#> 11 prod_kg_ha         Sete Lagoas  9532.    9.33
#> 12 prod_kg_ha         Viçosa       8816.    9.74

With ten or twenty measured traits, this form saves dozens of lines of repeated code.

7.3 pivot_wider(): from long to wide
The opposite direction is just as necessary. In breeding, the genotype × environment means table, with hybrids in rows and locations in columns, is the input to many adaptability and stability analyses (and is how results are usually shown in reports):

means_ge <- maize_2024 |>
  summarise(mean = mean(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(hibrido, local)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = local, values_from = mean)

means_ge
#> # A tibble: 20 × 5
#>    hibrido Londrina `Rio Verde` `Sete Lagoas` Viçosa
#>    <chr>      <dbl>       <dbl>         <dbl>  <dbl>
#>  1 HB01       9508       10735.         9814.  9293 
#>  2 HB02       8776        9567.        10035   7941.
#>  3 HB03       9842.      10609.         9820.  9130.
#>  4 HB04       8811.      10538          9777.  9329.
#>  5 HB05       9300.       9074.         8632   8813.
#>  6 HB06       8342        8492          8480.  8023.
#>  7 HB07       9649.       9808.         9944   8873 
#>  8 HB08       8961.      10150.         9226.  8270 
#>  9 HB09       9785.      10128.        10407   9199 
#> 10 HB10      10606       10378          9896   9284.
#> 11 HB11       7752.      10521.         9641   8894.
#> 12 HB12       8958       10288          8819   8892.
#> 13 HB13       9127.      11430          9120   8608.
#> 14 HB14       9477       10348.         9569   8872 
#> 15 HB15       7122        8989.         7430.  7133.
#> 16 HB16      10963.      10938         10782. 10357.
#> 17 HB17       9774.      11671         10227   9477.
#> 18 HB18       9580.      11579.         9533.  9274.
#> 19 HB19       8334.       9699.         9868   7496.
#> 20 HB20       9544.      10951          9839   9158

pivot_wider() needs two pieces of information: which column the new names come from (names_from) and which one the values come from (values_from). To use it as a numeric matrix, for example to compute correlations between environments:

ge_matrix <- means_ge |>
  column_to_rownames("hibrido") |>
  as.matrix()

round(cor(ge_matrix), 2)
#>             Londrina Rio Verde Sete Lagoas Viçosa
#> Londrina        1.00      0.51        0.69   0.81
#> Rio Verde       0.51      1.00        0.55   0.67
#> Sete Lagoas     0.69      0.55        1.00   0.66
#> Viçosa          0.81      0.67        0.66   1.00

Low correlations between two environments mean they rank the hybrids differently, a sign of genotype × environment interaction. We will come back to this in Module 5.

7.3.1 Useful pivot_wider() options

# A prefix on the new column names
maize |>
  summarise(mean = mean(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(hibrido, safra, local)) |>
  filter(local == "Viçosa") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = safra, values_from = mean, names_prefix = "season_") |>
  head(4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   hibrido local  `season_2023/24` `season_2024/25`
#>   <chr>   <chr>             <dbl>            <dbl>
#> 1 HB01    Viçosa            9293             9711 
#> 2 HB02    Viçosa            7941.            8157 
#> 3 HB03    Viçosa            9130.            8495.
#> 4 HB04    Viçosa            9329.            8161.

# Filling absent combinations with a value
tribble(
  ~hybrid, ~location, ~n,
  "HB01", "Viçosa", 3,
  "HB02", "Londrina", 2
) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = location, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   hybrid Viçosa Londrina
#>   <chr>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 HB01        3        0
#> 2 HB02        0        2

7.4 Splitting and joining columns
Compound identifiers are common in field sheets and genotyping files, such as "HB01-B2" for hybrid HB01 in block 2. unite() creates this kind of code and separate_wider_delim() undoes it:

plots <- maize_2024 |>
  select(local, hibrido, bloco, prod_kg_ha) |>
  unite("plot", hibrido, bloco, sep = "-B")

plots
#> # A tibble: 240 × 3
#>    local    plot    prod_kg_ha
#>    <chr>    <chr>        <dbl>
#>  1 Londrina HB01-B1       9779
#>  2 Londrina HB01-B2       9706
#>  3 Londrina HB01-B3       9039
#>  4 Londrina HB02-B1       8403
#>  5 Londrina HB02-B2       9430
#>  6 Londrina HB02-B3       8495
#>  7 Londrina HB03-B1      10545
#>  8 Londrina HB03-B2       9140
#>  9 Londrina HB03-B3         NA
#> 10 Londrina HB04-B1       7848
#> # ℹ 230 more rows

plots |>
  separate_wider_delim(plot, delim = "-B", names = c("hibrido", "bloco"))
#> # A tibble: 240 × 4
#>    local    hibrido bloco prod_kg_ha
#>    <chr>    <chr>   <chr>      <dbl>
#>  1 Londrina HB01    1           9779
#>  2 Londrina HB01    2           9706
#>  3 Londrina HB01    3           9039
#>  4 Londrina HB02    1           8403
#>  5 Londrina HB02    2           9430
#>  6 Londrina HB02    3           8495
#>  7 Londrina HB03    1          10545
#>  8 Londrina HB03    2           9140
#>  9 Londrina HB03    3             NA
#> 10 Londrina HB04    1           7848
#> # ℹ 230 more rows

Notice that bloco came back as text (<chr>): splitting columns always produces text. Convert it with mutate(bloco = as.integer(bloco)) when you need the number.
When the parts have a fixed width, separate_wider_position() cuts by position:

tibble(code = c("MG2023HB01", "GO2024HB15")) |>
  separate_wider_position(code, widths = c(state = 2, year = 4, hybrid = 4))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   state year  hybrid
#>   <chr> <chr> <chr> 
#> 1 MG    2023  HB01  
#> 2 GO    2024  HB15

For more complex patterns there is separate_wider_regex(), which uses regular expressions (lesson 8).

7.5 Missing values: explicit and implicit
A value can be missing in two ways:

explicitly: the row exists, but the cell is NA;
implicitly: the row simply does not exist.


# Simulate a file in which whoever typed it deleted the lost plots
maize_no_lost <- maize_2024 |>
  filter(!is.na(prod_kg_ha)) |>
  select(local, hibrido, bloco, prod_kg_ha)

nrow(maize_no_lost)
#> [1] 233

Rows are missing, but nothing in the table says which. complete() creates every combination of the given variables, filling with NA those that did not exist:

maize_complete <- maize_no_lost |>
  complete(local, hibrido, bloco)

nrow(maize_complete)
#> [1] 240
maize_complete |> filter(is.na(prod_kg_ha))
#> # A tibble: 7 × 4
#>   local       hibrido bloco prod_kg_ha
#>   <chr>       <chr>   <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 Londrina    HB03        3         NA
#> 2 Londrina    HB06        3         NA
#> 3 Londrina    HB14        3         NA
#> 4 Londrina    HB17        2         NA
#> 5 Londrina    HB20        1         NA
#> 6 Sete Lagoas HB01        1         NA
#> 7 Sete Lagoas HB10        1         NA

Making missing values explicit matters before analyses that assume a balanced design, and to document what was lost.
The other missing-value functions:

# drop_na(): removes rows with NA (in every column, or only in the ones given)
maize_complete |> drop_na(prod_kg_ha) |> nrow()
#> [1] 233

# replace_na(): replaces NA with a value (careful: zero is not the same as "not measured"!)
maize_2024 |> replace_na(list(obs = "no note")) |> count(obs)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   obs                 n
#>   <chr>           <int>
#> 1 acamamento         11
#> 2 no note           222
#> 3 parcela perdida     7

# fill(): repeats the last non-missing value, common in spreadsheets where the
# hybrid name is only written on the first row of each group
tribble(
  ~hybrid, ~block, ~yield,
  "HB01",  1,      9.1,
  NA,      2,      8.7,
  NA,      3,      9.4,
  "HB02",  1,      8.2,
  NA,      2,      8.5
) |>
  fill(hybrid)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   hybrid block yield
#>   <chr>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 HB01       1   9.1
#> 2 HB01       2   8.7
#> 3 HB01       3   9.4
#> 4 HB02       1   8.2
#> 5 HB02       2   8.5

7.7 Under the hood

7.7.1 The format depends on the tool



Tool
Expected format




dplyr, ggplot2, lm(), lme4, asreml
long (tidy)


cor(), prcomp(), matrix algebra, marker matrices
wide (matrix)


reports and spreadsheets for people
usually wide



That is why both pivot directions matter equally: data are stored tidy and widened only when a tool requires it.


7.7.2 What pivot_longer() does, step by step
pivot_longer() internally builds a specification stating, for each original column, which value it will have in the new names column. You can look at it and even edit it:

build_longer_spec(
  maize_2025_wide,
  cols = starts_with("prod_"),
  names_to = "local",
  names_prefix = "prod_",
  values_to = "prod_kg_ha"
)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   .name            .value     local      
#>   <chr>            <chr>      <chr>      
#> 1 prod_vicosa      prod_kg_ha vicosa     
#> 2 prod_sete_lagoas prod_kg_ha sete_lagoas
#> 3 prod_rio_verde   prod_kg_ha rio_verde  
#> 4 prod_londrina    prod_kg_ha londrina

For tricky cases (for example columns such as yield_2023, yield_2024, ht_2023, ht_2024), names_to accepts the special marker ".value", which keeps part of the name as a column:

tibble(hybrid = c("HB01", "HB02"),
       yield_2023 = c(9.1, 8.4), yield_2024 = c(9.6, 8.1),
       ht_2023 = c(220, 215),    ht_2024 = c(228, 211)) |>
  pivot_longer(-hybrid, names_to = c(".value", "year"), names_sep = "_")
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   hybrid year  yield    ht
#>   <chr>  <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 HB01   2023    9.1   220
#> 2 HB01   2024    9.6   228
#> 3 HB02   2023    8.4   215
#> 4 HB02   2024    8.1   211

7.8 Exercises

Tidy or not? For each table, say whether it is tidy and, if not, which rule it breaks: (a) a spreadsheet with columns hybrid, rep1, rep2, rep3 holding the yield of each replicate; (b) a table with columns hybrid, trait, value; (c) a location_year column with values such as "vicosa_2024".







TipSolution






No: “replicate” is a variable spread across the column names (breaks rule 1). Use pivot_longer(starts_with("rep"), names_to = "rep", names_prefix = "rep").
It depends on the question. If the observation is “one trait measured on one hybrid”, it is tidy; if the analysis treats each trait as a variable (for example, the correlation between yield and height), you need to widen it with pivot_wider().
No: two variables in one column (breaks rule 1). Use separate_wider_delim(location_year, "_", names = c("location", "year")).





Lengthen. The table below holds plant height at three assessment dates. Put it in long format, with a numeric days_after_sowing column.


heights <- tribble(
  ~hybrid, ~das_30, ~das_60, ~das_90,
  "HB01",  45,      130,     218,
  "HB02",  41,      122,     205,
  "HB03",  48,      138,     231
)







TipSolution






heights |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("das_"),
    names_to = "days_after_sowing",
    names_prefix = "das_",
    names_transform = as.integer,
    values_to = "height_cm"
  )
#> # A tibble: 9 × 3
#>   hybrid days_after_sowing height_cm
#>   <chr>              <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 HB01                  30        45
#> 2 HB01                  60       130
#> 3 HB01                  90       218
#> 4 HB02                  30        41
#> 5 HB02                  60       122
#> 6 HB02                  90       205
#> 7 HB03                  30        48
#> 8 HB03                  60       138
#> 9 HB03                  90       231

names_transform converts the names column, which would be text, into a number.




Widen. From maize (both seasons), build a table with one row per hybrid and one column for each combination of location and season, holding the mean yield. How many columns does it have?







TipSolution






maize |>
  summarise(mean = mean(prod_kg_ha, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(hibrido, local, safra)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = c(local, safra), values_from = mean) |>
  ncol()
#> [1] 9

One hybrid column plus 4 locations × 2 seasons = 9 columns. When names_from has two columns, the names are joined with _.




Implicit missing values. Use maize_no_lost and complete() to find how many plots were lost at each location.







TipSolution






maize_no_lost |>
  complete(local, hibrido, bloco) |>
  summarise(lost = sum(is.na(prod_kg_ha)), .by = local)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   local        lost
#>   <chr>       <int>
#> 1 Londrina        5
#> 2 Rio Verde       0
#> 3 Sete Lagoas     2
#> 4 Viçosa          0

Summary

Tidy data: each variable in a column, each observation in a row, each value in a cell.
pivot_longer() turns columns into rows (cols, names_to, values_to, names_prefix); pivot_wider() does the reverse (names_from, values_from).
Store data in long format and widen only when a tool demands it, as with the genotype × environment matrix.
separate_wider_delim() and unite() undo and create compound identifiers.
complete() makes implicit missing values explicit; drop_na(), replace_na() and fill() handle missing values deliberately.

text:
8.1 stringr: working with text






NotePackage intent: stringr



Problem it solves. Base R’s text functions (grepl(), sub(), gsub(), regmatches(), substr(), toupper()) have unhelpful names, different argument orders and inconsistent behaviour with NA.
Philosophy. In stringr, every function starts with str_ and takes the text as its first argument and the pattern as its second. That lets RStudio’s autocomplete work for you (type str_ and see the list) and fits every function into the pipe and mutate(). Under the hood it uses the stringi package, which handles accents and characters from any language correctly.
Why this one and not the alternatives. Base R does it all, but remembering whether it is grepl(pattern, x) or grepl(x, pattern) takes time and causes bugs. stringi is more complete but much larger; stringr gathers the everyday operations into about 50 consistent functions.



8.1.1 Diagnosis
Before cleaning, see exactly which variants exist:

soy |> count(cultivar) |> print(n = 40)
#> # A tibble: 38 × 2
#>    cultivar      n
#>    <chr>     <int>
#>  1 " SJ-01 "     1
#>  2 " SJ-02 "     1
#>  3 " SJ-06 "     1
#>  4 " SJ-08 "     1
#>  5 " SJ-14 "     1
#>  6 " SJ-15 "     1
#>  7 "SJ 01"       2
#>  8 "SJ 04"       1
#>  9 "SJ 10"       1
#> 10 "SJ 11"       2
#> 11 "SJ 12"       1
#> 12 "SJ 14"       1
#> 13 "SJ 15"       1
#> 14 "SJ-01"       4
#> 15 "SJ-02"       6
#> 16 "SJ-03"       8
#> 17 "SJ-04"       4
#> 18 "SJ-05"       8
#> 19 "SJ-06"       6
#> 20 "SJ-07"       6
#> 21 "SJ-08"       6
#> 22 "SJ-09"       7
#> 23 "SJ-10"       6
#> 24 "SJ-11"       6
#> 25 "SJ-12"       7
#> 26 "SJ-13"       8
#> 27 "SJ-14"       4
#> 28 "SJ-15"       5
#> 29 "sj-01"       1
#> 30 "sj-02"       1
#> 31 "sj-04"       3
#> 32 "sj-06"       1
#> 33 "sj-07"       2
#> 34 "sj-08"       1
#> 35 "sj-09"       1
#> 36 "sj-10"       1
#> 37 "sj-14"       2
#> 38 "sj-15"       1

There are four problems mixed together: leftover spaces (" SJ-01 "), lower case ("sj-01"), a space instead of the hyphen ("SJ 01") and combinations of these.


8.1.2 Cleaning step by step
Each problem has a function:

examples <- c(" SJ-01 ", "sj-01", "SJ 01", "SJ-01")

str_squish(examples)       # removes spaces at the ends and repeated spaces inside
#> [1] "SJ-01" "sj-01" "SJ 01" "SJ-01"
str_to_upper(examples)     # everything upper case
#> [1] " SJ-01 " "SJ-01"   "SJ 01"   "SJ-01"
str_replace(examples, " ", "-")   # replaces the first space with a hyphen
#> [1] "-SJ-01 " "sj-01"   "SJ-01"   "SJ-01"

Chained, in the right order:

examples |>
  str_squish() |>
  str_to_upper() |>
  str_replace(" ", "-")
#> [1] "SJ-01" "SJ-01" "SJ-01" "SJ-01"

Order matters: if we replaced spaces with hyphens before str_squish(), " SJ-01 " would become "-SJ-01-". Applied to the table:

soy <- soy |>
  mutate(cultivar = cultivar |> str_squish() |> str_to_upper() |> str_replace(" ", "-"))

soy |> count(cultivar)
#> # A tibble: 15 × 2
#>    cultivar     n
#>    <chr>    <int>
#>  1 SJ-01        8
#>  2 SJ-02        8
#>  3 SJ-03        8
#>  4 SJ-04        8
#>  5 SJ-05        8
#>  6 SJ-06        8
#>  7 SJ-07        8
#>  8 SJ-08        8
#>  9 SJ-09        8
#> 10 SJ-10        8
#> 11 SJ-11        8
#> 12 SJ-12        8
#> 13 SJ-13        8
#> 14 SJ-14        8
#> 15 SJ-15        8

Fifteen cultivars with eight plots each (2 locations × 4 blocks), as the design requires.


8.1.3 Other functions you will use a lot

codes <- c("SJ-01", "SJ-12", "HB-03", "SJ-7")

str_detect(codes, "SJ")          # contains "SJ"?
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE
str_starts(codes, "HB")          # starts with "HB"?
#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE
str_length(codes)                # number of characters
#> [1] 5 5 5 4
str_sub(codes, 1, 2)             # characters 1 to 2
#> [1] "SJ" "SJ" "HB" "SJ"
str_c("Cultivar ", codes)        # concatenate
#> [1] "Cultivar SJ-01" "Cultivar SJ-12" "Cultivar HB-03" "Cultivar SJ-7"
str_split_fixed(codes, "-", 2)   # split into two parts
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,] "SJ" "01"
#> [2,] "SJ" "12"
#> [3,] "HB" "03"
#> [4,] "SJ" "7"
str_pad(c("7", "12"), width = 2, pad = "0")   # left-pad with zeros
#> [1] "07" "12"

8.2 Essential regular expressions
A regular expression (regex) is a language for describing text patterns. You do not need to master it; a dozen symbols solve most trial-data cases:








Symbol
Meaning
Example




\\d
a digit
"\\d\\d" matches "07"


\\s
a space (or tab)



.
any character



+
one or more repetitions
"\\d+" matches "7" and "120"


*
zero or more repetitions



{n}
exactly n repetitions
"\\d{2}"


^ and $
start and end of the text
"^SJ" only matches at the start


[abc]
one of the listed characters
"[ -]" matches a space or a hyphen


( )
groups and captures



\|
or
"lost\|missing"



In R the backslash has to be written twice inside strings, hence \\d.

# Extract the cultivar number
str_extract(codes, "\\d+")
#> [1] "01" "12" "03" "7"

# Validate the format: two letters, hyphen, exactly two digits
str_detect(codes, "^[A-Z]{2}-\\d{2}$")
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE

# Fix: zero-pad a single-digit number at the end
str_replace(codes, "-(\\d)$", "-0\\1")
#> [1] "SJ-01" "SJ-12" "HB-03" "SJ-07"

In the last example, (\\d) captures the digit and \\1 puts it back in the replacement. Validation is good practice to leave in the cleaning script: if a code outside the pattern shows up in a future season, you find out immediately.

stopifnot(all(str_detect(soy$cultivar, "^SJ-\\d{2}$")))

stopifnot() does nothing if the condition is true and stops the script with an error if it is false. It is the simplest way to test your data inside the script itself.

8.2.1 Lodging

soy |> count(acamamento)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   acamamento     n
#>   <chr>      <int>
#> 1 NÃO            5
#> 2 Não           19
#> 3 SIM            1
#> 4 Sim            2
#> 5 não           82
#> 6 sim           11

soy <- soy |>
  mutate(acamamento = str_to_lower(acamamento) == "sim")

soy |> count(acamamento)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   acamamento     n
#>   <lgl>      <int>
#> 1 FALSE        106
#> 2 TRUE          14

We turned the column into a logical: TRUE if the plot lodged. Now mean(acamamento) directly gives the proportion of lodged plots.

8.3 forcats: controlling factors






NotePackage intent: forcats



Problem it solves. Factors are essential in models and plots, but reordering, renaming or merging levels in base R means manipulating levels() directly, which is easy to get wrong (remember the trap from lesson 3).
Philosophy. Every forcats function starts with fct_ and does one clear operation on the levels, never accidentally touching the observations’ values: reorder by another variable (fct_reorder), by frequency (fct_infreq), by hand (fct_relevel); rename (fct_recode); lump rare levels (fct_lump_n).
Why this one and not the alternatives. The same operations are possible with factor(x, levels = ...) and levels(x) <- ..., but with a real risk of swapping the observations’ labels. forcats is part of the tidyverse and was built precisely to make these operations safe.



soy <- soy |>
  mutate(
    local = factor(local),
    cultivar = factor(cultivar),
    bloco = factor(bloco)
  )

levels(soy$local)
#> [1] "Rio Verde" "Viçosa"


8.3.1 Reordering
By default levels are in alphabetical order. In tables and plots it is almost always more useful to order by a statistic. fct_reorder() orders a factor’s levels by the values of another variable:

soy <- soy |>
  mutate(cultivar = fct_reorder(cultivar, produtividade_sc_ha, .fun = median, .na_rm = TRUE))

levels(soy$cultivar)   # from the lowest to the highest median yield
#>  [1] "SJ-05" "SJ-04" "SJ-01" "SJ-12" "SJ-06" "SJ-03" "SJ-11" "SJ-14" "SJ-02"
#> [10] "SJ-07" "SJ-09" "SJ-15" "SJ-13" "SJ-08" "SJ-10"

In lesson 19 this will be the trick for ordered bar charts. Other ways to reorder:

fct_relevel(soy$local, "Viçosa") |> levels()   # moves one level to the front
#> [1] "Viçosa"    "Rio Verde"
fct_rev(soy$local) |> levels()                 # reverses the order
#> [1] "Viçosa"    "Rio Verde"
fct_infreq(c("b", "a", "b", "c", "b", "a")) |> levels()   # by frequency
#> [1] "b" "a" "c"

fct_relevel() matters in models: the first level is the reference for contrasts in lm(). If the trial’s check cultivar is SJ-15, putting it first makes the coefficients measure each cultivar’s difference from the check.


8.3.2 Renaming and lumping

soy |>
  mutate(local = fct_recode(local, "Viçosa (MG)" = "Viçosa", "Rio Verde (GO)" = "Rio Verde")) |>
  count(local)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   local              n
#>   <fct>          <int>
#> 1 Rio Verde (GO)    60
#> 2 Viçosa (MG)       60

# Keeps the 2 most frequent levels and lumps the rest into "Other"
fct_lump_n(c("SJ-01", "SJ-01", "SJ-02", "SJ-03", "SJ-03", "SJ-03", "SJ-04"), n = 2, other_level = "Other")
#> [1] SJ-01 SJ-01 Other SJ-03 SJ-03 SJ-03 Other
#> Levels: SJ-01 SJ-03 Other



8.3.3 Empty levels

only_vicosa <- soy |> filter(local == "Viçosa")
levels(only_vicosa$local)              # Rio Verde is still a level
#> [1] "Rio Verde" "Viçosa"
levels(fct_drop(only_vicosa$local))    # fct_drop() removes levels with no observations
#> [1] "Viçosa"

8.4 lubridate: dates






NotePackage intent: lubridate



Problem it solves. Dates arrive in varied formats (22/10/2023, 2023-10-22, 22-Oct-2023) and base R requires you to spell out the format with codes such as "%d/%m/%Y". Computing intervals, adding days or extracting the month also takes a different function for each case.
Philosophy. In lubridate, the function name describes the order of the date components: dmy() for day-month-year, ymd() for year-month-day, mdy() for the US format. It recognises separators automatically and offers obviously named functions to extract parts (year(), month(), yday()) and to add periods (days(), months()).
Why this one and not the alternatives. as.Date(x, format = "%d/%m/%Y") works and is what lubridate does underneath, but it fails on mixed formats and requires memorising the codes. For field data, where the same spreadsheet has dates typed in different ways, lubridate saves a lot of work.



dmy("22/10/2023")
#> [1] "2023-10-22"
dmy("22-10-2023")
#> [1] "2023-10-22"
dmy("22 October 2023")
#> [1] "2023-10-22"
ymd("2023-10-22")
#> [1] "2023-10-22"

A date in R is a number of days since 1 January 1970, with class Date:

date <- dmy("22/10/2023")
class(date)
#> [1] "Date"
as.numeric(date)
#> [1] 19652


8.4.1 Mixed formats
The sowing column has the formats dd/mm/yyyy and yyyy-mm-dd. dmy() alone would fail on the latter. parse_date_time() takes a list of possible formats and tries each one:

soy |> count(str_detect(data_de_semeadura, "/"))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   `str_detect(data_de_semeadura, "/")`     n
#>   <lgl>                                <int>
#> 1 FALSE                                   23
#> 2 TRUE                                    97

soy <- soy |>
  mutate(sowing_date = as_date(parse_date_time(data_de_semeadura, orders = c("dmy", "ymd")))) |>
  select(-data_de_semeadura)

soy |> count(local, sowing_date)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   local     sowing_date     n
#>   <fct>     <date>      <int>
#> 1 Rio Verde 2024-10-27     20
#> 2 Rio Verde 2024-10-28     20
#> 3 Rio Verde 2024-10-29     20
#> 4 Viçosa    2024-10-15     22
#> 5 Viçosa    2024-10-16     19
#> 6 Viçosa    2024-10-17     19
sum(is.na(soy$sowing_date))
#> [1] 0

No dates lost, and the sowing dates at each location are close together, as expected.






WarningAmbiguous formats



Is "03/04/2024" 3 April (Brazilian and European convention) or 4 March (US convention)? No function can guess. When there are dates like this, confirm the convention with whoever typed the data and use a single format in orders. parse_date_time() with several formats is safe here because dmy and ymd can never be confused (the four-digit year sits in different positions).




8.4.2 Computing with dates

soy <- soy |>
  mutate(
    maturity_date = sowing_date + days(dias_ate_maturacao),
    maturity_month = month(maturity_date),
    sowing_day_of_year = yday(sowing_date)
  )

soy |>
  select(local, cultivar, sowing_date, dias_ate_maturacao, maturity_date, maturity_month) |>
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   local  cultivar sowing_date dias_ate_maturacao maturity_date maturity_month
#>   <fct>  <fct>    <date>                   <dbl> <date>                 <dbl>
#> 1 Viçosa SJ-01    2024-10-16                 131 2025-02-24                 2
#> 2 Viçosa SJ-01    2024-10-16                 119 2025-02-12                 2
#> 3 Viçosa SJ-01    2024-10-17                 113 2025-02-07                 2
#> 4 Viçosa SJ-01    2024-10-15                 109 2025-02-01                 2
#> 5 Viçosa SJ-02    2024-10-15                 118 2025-02-10                 2
#> 6 Viçosa SJ-02    2024-10-16                 118 2025-02-11                 2

The difference between two dates is a time interval:

dmy("15/02/2025") - dmy("15/10/2024")
#> Time difference of 123 days
as.numeric(dmy("15/02/2025") - dmy("15/10/2024"))
#> [1] 123

The most used extraction functions: year(), month(), day(), yday() (day of the year, useful to compare sowing times across years), wday() (day of the week) and week().

8.5 Deliberate missing values

# na_if(): turns a code value into NA (for example, 0 typed instead of "not measured")
c(15.2, 0, 16.1, 0, 14.8) |> na_if(0)
#> [1] 15.2   NA 16.1   NA 14.8

# coalesce(): uses the first non-missing value across several columns
coalesce(c(NA, 15.2, NA), c(14.9, 15.0, NA), c(0, 0, 0))
#> [1] 14.9 15.2  0.0

# if_any() / if_all(): conditions over several columns at once
soy |>
  filter(if_any(c(produtividade_sc_ha, peso_100_sementes_g), is.na)) |>
  select(local, cultivar, bloco, produtividade_sc_ha, peso_100_sementes_g)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 5

8.6 The clean soybean trial
Putting everything into a single pipeline, which will be the template for the cleaning script in lesson 9:

soy_clean <- read_delim(
  here("data", "raw", "soja_ensaio_2025.csv"),
  delim = ";",
  locale = locale(decimal_mark = ",", encoding = "latin1"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    cultivar = cultivar |> str_squish() |> str_to_upper() |> str_replace(" ", "-"),
    acamamento = str_to_lower(acamamento) == "sim",

8.7 Under the hood

8.7.1 Text encoding
Every string in R has an encoding. After reading with locale(encoding = "latin1"), readr converted everything to UTF-8:

Encoding("Viçosa")
#> [1] "UTF-8"
utf8ToInt("ç")          # the character's Unicode code point
#> [1] 231
charToRaw("Viçosa")     # the bytes: "ç" takes two in UTF-8
#> [1] 56 69 c3 a7 6f 73 61

If you ever need to compare strings with and without accents (for example "Vicosa" and "Viçosa"), strip the accents explicitly:

stringi::stri_trans_general("Viçosa, São Paulo", "Latin-ASCII")
#> [1] "Vicosa, Sao Paulo"



8.7.2 Dates and time zones
parse_date_time() returns a POSIXct (date and time), which is why we used as_date() to keep only the date. Date-times carry a time zone, which can shift the day in a careless conversion. For daily field data, always work with Date.

parse_date_time("2024-10-15", "ymd")
#> [1] "2024-10-15 UTC"
as_date(parse_date_time("2024-10-15", "ymd"))
#> [1] "2024-10-15"

8.8 Exercises

Locations with different spellings. Standardise the vector c("Viçosa", "VIÇOSA", " viçosa", "Vicosa", "Rio Verde", "rio  verde") to "Viçosa" and "Rio Verde". Hint: str_to_title() and str_replace().







TipSolution






locations <- c("Viçosa", "VIÇOSA", " viçosa", "Vicosa", "Rio Verde", "rio  verde")

locations |>
  str_squish() |>
  str_to_title() |>
  str_replace("^Vicosa$", "Viçosa")
#> [1] "Viçosa"    "Viçosa"    "Viçosa"    "Viçosa"    "Rio Verde" "Rio Verde"

str_to_title() capitalises the first letter of each word. The spelling without the cedilla needs an explicit fix, because no general rule knows that “Vicosa” should have one.




Regex. From the vector c("HB01-B1", "HB12-B3", "HB7-B2", "hb05-b1"), extract the hybrid number (as a number) and the block number, and identify which codes do not follow the pattern HB + two digits + -B + one digit.







TipSolution






plots <- c("HB01-B1", "HB12-B3", "HB7-B2", "hb05-b1")

str_extract(plots, "(?i)hb(\\d+)", group = 1) |> as.integer()
#> [1]  1 12  7  5
str_extract(plots, "(?i)b(\\d)$", group = 1) |> as.integer()
#> [1] 1 3 2 1
plots[!str_detect(plots, "^HB\\d{2}-B\\d$")]
#> [1] "HB7-B2"  "hb05-b1"

(?i) at the start of the pattern ignores case; group = 1 returns only what the parentheses captured.




The check as reference. In the clean soybean trial, make SJ-15 the first level of cultivar and check with levels(). Why would this change the coefficients of lm(produtividade_sc_ha ~ cultivar)?







TipSolution






soy_clean <- soy_clean |> mutate(cultivar = fct_relevel(cultivar, "SJ-15"))
levels(soy_clean$cultivar)[1:3]
#> [1] "SJ-15" "SJ-01" "SJ-02"

In lm(), the first level becomes the reference: the intercept becomes the mean of SJ-15 and each coefficient the difference between a cultivar and SJ-15. Fitted values and the F test do not change; only the interpretation of the coefficients does.




Maize dates. In the 2023/24 maize trial (lesson 5), the data_plantio (planting date) column is text in dd/mm/yyyy format. Convert it to a date and compute each plot’s likely flowering date by adding florescimento_dias. In which month did most plots flower?







TipSolution






maize_file <- here("data", "raw", "milho_met_2024.xlsx")

readxl::excel_sheets(maize_file) |>
  set_names() |>
  map(\(sheet) readxl::read_excel(maize_file, sheet = sheet, skip = 3, na = c("", "-", "perdida"))) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "local") |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    data_plantio = dmy(data_plantio),
    flowering_date = data_plantio + days(florescimento_dias)
  ) |>
  count(month = month(flowering_date))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   month     n
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1     3
#> 2    12   237

text:
9.1 What the “Zen of R” is
Throughout this module we have built up a set of habits. Together they make up what the Brazilian R community calls the Zen of R (O Zen do R) (Trecenti and Lente 2021): a way of organising work so that it is reproducible, readable and easy to pick up again. The principles we adopt in the lab:

Everything is a project. A folder, a .Rproj, a Git repository (lesson 1).
Relative paths with here(), never setwd() (lesson 1).
Raw data are sacred. data/raw/ is read-only; every correction is code (lesson 5).
Code is the source of truth. No .RData; any result must be recreated by running the scripts in a clean session (lesson 1).
Recorded versions with renv (lesson 4).
Readable code: consistent style, descriptive names, small functions (this lesson).
Full history with Git (this lesson).

This lesson closes the module by making all these principles work together.

9.2 Code style
Code is read far more often than it is written, and almost always by someone else (or by you, months later, which is practically someone else). A consistent style cuts the effort of reading. The lab follows the tidyverse style guide, whose main rules you have already been practising:








Rule
Yes
No




Names in snake_case
prod_kg_ha, read_soy_2025()
ProdKgHa, read.soy()


<- to assign
x <- 5
x = 5


Spaces around operators and after commas
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
mean(x,na.rm=TRUE)


One pipe step per line
x |> ↵ filter()
everything on one long line


Lines up to 80 characters




Two-space indentation

tabs



Nobody needs to memorise spacing rules: two tools do it for you.






NotePackage intent: styler and lintr



Problem they solve. Reviewing style by hand is tedious, subjective and pulls attention away from what matters in a code review: the logic.
Philosophy. The two work together, with complementary roles. styler fixes formatting automatically (spaces, indentation, line breaks) without changing what the code does. lintr points out problems that need a human decision, such as names off the standard, long lines, unused objects or using = to assign.
Why these and not the alternatives. They are the community’s reference tools, configured by default for the tidyverse guide, integrated into RStudio (the Addins menu) and into GitHub Actions. The alternative, an IDE’s own formatter, is not standardised across editors and checks neither names nor logic.



messy_code <- "average<-function(x,drop_na=TRUE){
if(drop_na){x=x[!is.na(x)]}
sum( x )/length(x)}"

styler::style_text(messy_code)
#> Warning: Could not use `colored = TRUE`, as the package prettycode is not installed.
#> Please install it if you want to see colored output or see
#> `?styler::print.vertical()` for more information.
#> average <- function(x, drop_na = TRUE) {
#>   if (drop_na) {
#>     x <- x[!is.na(x)]
#>   }
#>   sum(x) / length(x)
#> }

styler reorganised indentation, spaces and braces, and replaced = with <-, without changing what the function does. For a file or for the whole project:

styler::style_file("scripts/A01_preparar_dados.R")
styler::style_dir("scripts")

lintr produces a diagnosis, line by line:

lintr::lint(
  text = "OverallMean = mean(maize$prod_kg_ha,na.rm=T)\n",
  linters = lintr::linters_with_defaults()
)
#> <text>:1:1: style: [object_name_linter] Variable and function name style should match snake_case or symbols.
#> OverallMean = mean(maize$prod_kg_ha,na.rm=T)
#> ^~~~~~~~~~~
#> <text>:1:13: style: [assignment_linter] Use <- for assignment, not =.
#> OverallMean = mean(maize$prod_kg_ha,na.rm=T)
#>             ^
#> <text>:1:37: style: [commas_linter] Put a space after a comma.
#> OverallMean = mean(maize$prod_kg_ha,na.rm=T)
#>                                     ^
#> <text>:1:42: style: [infix_spaces_linter] Put spaces around all infix operators.
#> OverallMean = mean(maize$prod_kg_ha,na.rm=T)
#>                                          ^
#> <text>:1:44: style: [T_and_F_symbol_linter] Use TRUE instead of the symbol T.
#> OverallMean = mean(maize$prod_kg_ha,na.rm=T)
#>                                           ~^

Note the warning about T: T and F are just objects worth TRUE and FALSE, and they can be overwritten (T <- 0). Always write TRUE and FALSE in full.






TipIn RStudio



Addins > Style active file applies styler to the open file, and Ctrl + Shift + A reformats the selection. For lintr, run lintr::lint("file.R") and the warnings show up in the Markers pane, with links to each line.
